def factorial(n):

findings: Background

Chapter 5 of the 3rd edition teaches four ways to find and prevent bugs: raising an exception with the raise statement and catching it with except, assertions that check a condition the programmer believes is true, the logging module with its five levels and its options for a file and for switching messages off, and the debugger of the Mu editor with its Continue, Step In, Step Over, Step Out and Stop controls and its breakpoints, closing with a buggy adding program, a coin flip program and the practice program Buggy Coin Toss Game.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's printed behaviours reproduce under Python 3.14.4: box_print raises the messages the chapter shows for a width of 1 and a two-character symbol, a failing assert raises AssertionError with an empty message, the level names carry the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, the factorial with range(n + 1) returns 0 and the fixed one 120, and the adding program prints 5342 instead of 50 until its answers are converted with int.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's advice that assertions are for programmer errors follows from how the interpreter treats them: assert expression is equivalent to raising AssertionError only when __debug__ is true, and a program run with the -O option, or code compiled with optimisation, contains no assertion at all, so an assert must never carry a check the program needs to perform on user input.
Comparative analysis

The chapter presents logging as a replacement for print calls, and the documentation adds what makes it more than that: the default level is WARNING so debug and info calls print nothing until basicConfig lowers the threshold, basicConfig does nothing when the root logger already has handlers unless force=True is given, logging.disable(level) silences that level and every lower one until it is called with NOTSET, and a call that passes arguments to the message formats them only if the message is emitted.
Comparative analysis

The debugger the chapter describes belongs to the Mu editor, whose five controls correspond to commands of the standard library debugger pdb - step, next, return, continue and break - so the same technique is available in any Python installation, and since Python 3.7 a program can start it with the built-in breakpoint(), which calls sys.breakpointhook and is switched off by setting PYTHONBREAKPOINT to 0.
Comparative analysis

Executing the chapter's debugging behaviours under Python 3.12.11 and 3.14.4 shows where the two differ. The pdb stops for the same program are identical, but a program that calls breakpoint() stops on the call line under 3.14 and on the next line under 3.12; the message of random.randint(2, 1) is empty range in randint(2, 1) under 3.14 and empty range in randrange(2, 2) under 3.12; the caret marks of a traceback differ; and sys.remote_exec, with python -m pdb -p, exists only from 3.14. The command r of pdb stops on the return line of a function, printing --Return-- and the value, and not in the calling code; the chapter's Step Out is described as running until the function is left. Every one of these was executed, and the corpus states them as version-dependent where they are.
Conclusion

For an advanced course, chapter 5 is best taught as a choice among four instruments by the question asked: raise when the caller can do something about the error, assert when the programmer's belief must hold, log when the run must leave a record, and step through with the debugger when the state at one point is the question; the chapter's printed outputs hold under 3.14.4, and optimised mode, lazy formatting, force=True, breakpoint(), remote attachment, fine-grained tracebacks and exception notes are what the chapter leaves for the course to add.
Contemporary developments

Python 3.14 added to debugging a safe way to attach the debugger to a running process, python -m pdb -p followed by the process identifier, built on sys.remote_exec of PEP 768, and lets a hardcoded breakpoint() reuse the last debugger instance so that its breakpoints and settings persist between stops.
Contemporary developments

Since Python 3.11 a traceback points at the failing expression inside a line with carets, so the failing subscript in a chained lookup can be seen without a debugger, and any exception can carry notes added with add_note, which are printed after the traceback and kept in __notes__, so code that catches and re-raises can say where in the work the error occurred.
Terms used without definition

The chapter text names ideas that it never explains and that a learner of the course could not look up in the corpus itself: the word bug, which it uses throughout without defining it; the Exception() function and the error message passed to it, which it does not link to the class of the exception; the list ages with its sort() and reverse() methods; the format string with its %(asctime)s fields; the named parameter filename; the augmented assignment total *= i; the range that starts at 0; the tuple and the not in test of the practice program; the string that input() returns; and the Mu editor with its Debug Inspector pane. The Python glossary defines object, class, attribute, method, mapping, docstring, bytecode and file object; the tutorial on data structures defines the tuple and its comma; the tutorial on input and output defines the file, its modes and its encoding; the language reference defines the membership test and the default comparison of unrelated types; the library pages define random.randint, os.environ, os.getpid, subprocess, __debug__ and the IDLE debugger. Version 1.1.0 of the corpus gives each of these a concept, or a place in the explanation of one, and renews the chapter text as four to six paragraphs for every concept.
title: Debugging for an advanced course: chapter 5 of the 3rd edition and today's Python

nodes.label: Bugs and debugging
nodes.body: A bug is a place where a program does something other than what its author meant it to do, and debugging is the work of finding and removing such places. Chapter 5 opens with the observation that once a learner can write basic programs, the bugs become less simple, and it offers tools and techniques for finding the root cause of a bug quickly and with little effort (Sweigart, 2025). This branch collects the ideas that sit underneath those tools: what a bug is, how bugs differ from one another, what debugging asks of the programmer, and how to choose the right tool for a given question.

paras.text: A bug is a place where a program does something other than what its author meant it to do, and debugging is the work of finding and removing such places. Chapter 5 opens with the observation that once a learner can write basic programs, the bugs become less simple, and it offers tools and techniques for finding the root cause of a bug quickly and with little effort (Sweigart, 2025). This branch collects the ideas that sit underneath those tools: what a bug is, how bugs differ from one another, what debugging asks of the programmer, and how to choose the right tool for a given question.

Every programmer writes bugs, however experienced. The chapter quotes the old joke that writing code accounts for 90 percent of programming while debugging accounts for the other 90 percent, and it reminds the reader that a computer does only what it is told and will not read the programmer's mind (Sweigart, 2025). A learner who treats debugging as an ordinary, learnable activity, and not as a sign of failure, finds bugs faster and loses less confidence while doing so.

The ideas of this branch apply to every program in the course, from a ten-line exercise to the capstone project. They are placed first in the chapter's concept tree because the four groups that follow, raising exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger, are four answers to one question: how can the programmer find out what the program is really doing, as opposed to what its source code appears to say?

The branch has three parts. The first describes the nature of a bug, with the bug itself, the logic error that produces a wrong answer without any complaint from Python, and the process of debugging. The second explains how to choose among the four instruments by the question that is being asked. The third, the working vocabulary, explains objects, the command line and files, which the tools take for granted. The chapter gives the guiding rule in its introduction: in general, the earlier a bug is caught, the easier it is to fix (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.label: Nature of a bug
nodes.body: The nature of a bug concerns what kind of thing a bug is and how it shows itself. Python distinguishes errors that stop a program before it starts, errors that stop it while it runs, and mistakes that do not stop it at all. The first two are reported by the interpreter, and the third is noticed only by a person who sees that the result is wrong.

paras.text: The nature of a bug concerns what kind of thing a bug is and how it shows itself. Python distinguishes errors that stop a program before it starts, errors that stop it while it runs, and mistakes that do not stop it at all. The first two are reported by the interpreter, and the third is noticed only by a person who sees that the result is wrong.

Knowing which of the three kinds one is facing decides what to do next. A message from Python names a line to look at, whereas a silently wrong answer gives no line at all, and the programmer must observe the program's behaviour to find the cause. The chapter's two practice programs, a factorial that returns 0 and an adding program that prints 5342, are both of the silent kind (Sweigart, 2025).

The next three concepts take the three kinds in turn: the bug as a gap between intention and behaviour, the logic error that hides behind a program that runs normally, and debugging as the method by which the gap is located and closed.

The three kinds separate cleanly on tests a learner can run. A file with a mistyped keyword never reaches its first line at all, because Python compiles the whole file before running any of it; a line such as int('hello') stops the program while it runs, with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'; and a factorial whose accumulator starts at 0 instead of 1 prints 0 for every input and is wrong for all of them (Sweigart, 2025). The first two name a line to look at and the third names nothing, which is the whole reason this chapter's instruments exist.

nodes.label: Bug
nodes.body: A bug is a defect in a program: a line, a missing line or a wrong assumption that makes the program behave differently from what its author intended. The word describes the gap between the intention in the programmer's head and the behaviour of the running program, and not the computer, which carries out every instruction exactly as written. As the chapter puts it, the computer does only what it is told to do, and it will not read the programmer's mind (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A bug is a defect in a program: a line, a missing line or a wrong assumption that makes the program behave differently from what its author intended. The word describes the gap between the intention in the programmer's head and the behaviour of the running program, and not the computer, which carries out every instruction exactly as written. As the chapter puts it, the computer does only what it is told to do, and it will not read the programmer's mind (Sweigart, 2025).

The idea matters because it moves the blame to where the repair can happen. A programmer who believes that the computer is wrong looks in the wrong place, whereas a programmer who accepts that the instructions were not the intended ones starts reading them critically. The chapter adds that even professional programmers create bugs all the time, so a learner should not be discouraged by them (Sweigart, 2025).

Bugs are met in every program a learner writes. The chapter's first example is a function that computes the factorial of 5, the product 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 x 5, which should be 120. Its loop starts at 0 instead of 1, so the first multiplication multiplies by zero and every later step keeps the total at zero, and the function returns 0 (Sweigart, 2025).

The effect can be reproduced by hand. The expression 1 * 0 * 1 * 2 * 3 * 4 * 5, which is the sequence of multiplications that the faulty loop performs, evaluates to 0, because any number multiplied by zero is zero. Nothing in the program is syntactically wrong and no rule of the language is broken, so Python has no reason to complain; the defect exists only relative to what the author wanted.

Not every surprising result is a bug in the program: sometimes the author's expectation is wrong. Before changing code, state precisely what the correct result should be and why. Equally, a program that produces the expected output for one input may still contain a bug that shows itself on another, so a bug is confirmed or ruled out by testing more than one case.

nodes.definition: A place where a program does something other than what its author intended; the chapter's factorial multiplies by 0 and so returns 0 instead of 120.

nodes.label: Logic error
nodes.body: A logic error is a mistake in the reasoning of a program that lets it run to the end without raising any exception and yet produces a wrong result. It is different from a syntax error, which the Python tutorial describes as a parsing error that stops the program from starting, and from an exception, which the tutorial defines as an error detected during execution (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A logic error produces neither complaint, and so the interpreter is silent about it.

paras.text: A logic error is a mistake in the reasoning of a program that lets it run to the end without raising any exception and yet produces a wrong result. It is different from a syntax error, which the Python tutorial describes as a parsing error that stops the program from starting, and from an exception, which the tutorial defines as an error detected during execution (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A logic error produces neither complaint, and so the interpreter is silent about it.

Logic errors are the hardest bugs to find because nothing points at them. The chapter's adding program shows this clearly: the author remarks that the program has not crashed, but the sum is obviously wrong (Sweigart, 2025). The program's output looks plausible to the interpreter and implausible only to a person who knows what the answer should be.

The chapter contains two logic errors. The factorial function returns 0 because its loop begins at the wrong number, and the adding program prints The sum is 5342 for the inputs 5, 3 and 42, because input returns strings and the plus sign joins strings instead of adding numbers (Sweigart, 2025). The coin toss practice program at the end of the chapter contains further ones.

Finding a logic error is a matter of making the program show its inner state. The three tools that follow in the chapter do this in different ways: log messages print values as the program runs, assertions check beliefs about values, and the debugger lets the programmer stop the program and read the values. In the adding program, converting each answer with int changes the output from The sum is 5342 to The sum is 50.

A passing run is not proof of correctness. A logic error can hide for as long as the test inputs happen not to touch it, so the cheapest defence is to test with inputs whose answers are known in advance and to compare them with what the program prints.

nodes.definition: A mistake that lets the program run to the end without any exception but produces a wrong result, so only the person who knows the right answer can notice it.

nodes.label: Debugging
nodes.body: Debugging is the activity of finding the root cause of a bug and removing it. The chapter introduces it as a set of tools and techniques that identify exactly what the code is doing and where it is going wrong (Sweigart, 2025). The root cause is the earliest point at which the program's behaviour departs from the programmer's intention, and not the place where the wrong result is finally printed.

paras.text: Debugging is the activity of finding the root cause of a bug and removing it. The chapter introduces it as a set of tools and techniques that identify exactly what the code is doing and where it is going wrong (Sweigart, 2025). The root cause is the earliest point at which the program's behaviour departs from the programmer's intention, and not the place where the wrong result is finally printed.

A systematic method saves time compared with changing code at random. The chapter notes that the debugger runs a program much more slowly than normal, but lets the programmer see the actual values in a program while it runs, instead of deducing them from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Seeing replaces guessing, and that is the central idea of debugging.

Debugging is done at every stage of development: while writing a function and testing it on one input, after a bug report from a user, and while reading someone else's code. The four instruments of the chapter correspond to four moments of this work: a function can refuse bad input with a raised exception, a program can state its beliefs with assertions, a program can leave a record with log messages, and the programmer can stop it with a debugger.

A debugging session follows a loop: reproduce the wrong behaviour, look at the program's state at a suitable point, guess the cause, change one thing and run again. The cheapest way to look at the state is a print of the loop's variables. A loop that multiplies a total by i over range(5 + 1) prints 0 0, 1 0, 2 0, 3 0, 4 0 and 5 0 for i and total, and the first line already reveals that i starts at zero.

Change one thing at a time, and run the program again after each change; two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one mattered. Remove the temporary prints when the bug is found, or use logging, which the chapter recommends for the reason that its messages can be switched off in one place (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.example: printing i and total in the loop
nodes.definition: The method of finding the root cause of a bug by making the program show its state, forming a guess about the cause and testing it.

nodes.label: Instrument selection
nodes.body: Instrument selection is the choice of which of the chapter's four tools suits a given question. The chapter closes its summary by listing them together: assertions, exceptions, logging and the debugger are all valuable tools to find and prevent bugs (Sweigart, 2025). They overlap but they are not interchangeable, because each answers a different question about a program.

paras.text: Instrument selection is the choice of which of the chapter's four tools suits a given question. The chapter closes its summary by listing them together: assertions, exceptions, logging and the debugger are all valuable tools to find and prevent bugs (Sweigart, 2025). They overlap but they are not interchangeable, because each answers a different question about a program.

A learner who knows only one tool will use it for everything, filling a program with print calls or stepping through a thousand iterations by hand. Matching the tool to the question saves effort and avoids the characteristic misuse of each, such as an assertion that checks what a user types.
The next concept states the rule of choice in a sentence for each tool. The branches that follow in the concept tree then explain each tool in turn, beginning with the raise statement.

The rule of choice can be put as four questions. What a program did across many passes is answered by logging, because the messages stay in the output and can carry a time; the state of one pass is answered by the debugger, because the program can be halted and its variables read; whether a condition the programmer believes could ever fail is answered by an assertion; and what a function should do with an argument it cannot use is answered by raising (Sweigart, 2025). The characteristic misuse of each follows from asking it the wrong question, and the sharpest case is an assertion standing in for a check on what a user typed, since running the file with python -O removes every assertion and leaves no check at all.

nodes.label: Choosing by question
nodes.body: Choosing an instrument means asking what the problem is and then picking the tool built for that kind of problem. The chapter's summary supplies the material: assertions are a good way to implement sanity checks that give early warning when a necessary condition does not hold, an exception can be caught and handled by try and except statements, the logging module looks into the code while it runs, and the debugger steps through the program one line at a time (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Choosing an instrument means asking what the problem is and then picking the tool built for that kind of problem. The chapter's summary supplies the material: assertions are a good way to implement sanity checks that give early warning when a necessary condition does not hold, an exception can be caught and handled by try and except statements, the logging module looks into the code while it runs, and the debugger steps through the program one line at a time (Sweigart, 2025).

The choice matters because each tool has a cost and a purpose. An exception is part of the program's normal behaviour and the user can meet it. An assertion is a check for the programmer, and the chapter says a user should never see an assertion error in a finished program. A log message costs a call but can be switched off with one line, and the debugger costs time at every step.

In practice the four tools appear in the same program. A function validates its arguments and raises an exception when the caller made a mistake. An assertion checks an internal result such as a sorted list. Log messages describe the path a long run takes, and the debugger is brought in for the one place where the values still puzzle the programmer.

The rule of thumb, which this course states in four sentences, is as follows. Raise an exception when the caller can do something about the error. Assert a condition that must be true if the program is correct. Log when a run must leave a record that can be read after it ends. Step through with the debugger when the question is about the state at one particular line. Each sentence has a concept of its own later in this chapter.

The sentences describe tendencies and not laws. A logged message about a user error is often worth keeping next to the exception that reports it, and a debugger session often ends with a new assertion added to keep the bug from returning. Do not use an assertion for a user error, because assertions can be removed from a running program, which a later concept explains.

nodes.example: raise, assert, log or step through?
nodes.definition: Raise when the caller can react to the error, assert when the programmer's belief must hold, log when the run must leave a record, and use the debugger when the state at one point is the question.

nodes.label: Working vocabulary
nodes.body: The working vocabulary gathers three everyday ideas that the chapter's tools take for granted: objects with their attributes and methods, the command line, and files with the directories that hold them. None of them is a tool for finding bugs. Each is needed to read the sentences in which the tools are described, such as the exception stores its arguments in an attribute, run the program with python -m pdb, or the log messages are written to a file.

paras.text: The working vocabulary gathers three everyday ideas that the chapter's tools take for granted: objects with their attributes and methods, the command line, and files with the directories that hold them. None of them is a tool for finding bugs. Each is needed to read the sentences in which the tools are described, such as the exception stores its arguments in an attribute, run the program with python -m pdb, or the log messages are written to a file.

A reader who does not know these words meets them everywhere in the rest of the chapter and in the Python documentation, which uses them without comment. The glossary of the documentation defines them in a line or two, and the course builds on those definitions. Knowing them also removes a source of confusion in debugging itself: a program started from a button of an editor and the same program started from the command line can differ in options and in environment, and a log file that was written in one directory is not found in another.

The three concepts take the ideas in turn. The first explains objects, classes, attributes and methods, the vocabulary of every exception, logger and record. The second explains the command line, with its options and arguments, which controls how Python and its debugger are started. The third explains files, their modes, and directories, which the logging branch relies on when it writes a log file. Each has a short executed example.

Each of the three can be shown in a line of real Python. An exception is an object, so a handler may read its text with str and the values it was built from in its args attribute, which for int('hello') is a one-item tuple holding that message. A program is started from the command line with options that change what it does, so python -m pdb starts a file under the debugger while python -O strips its assertions (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A log file is an ordinary file opened in append mode, which is why a second run of the program adds to it instead of replacing what the first run wrote.

nodes.label: Objects, attributes and methods
nodes.body: An object, in the words of the glossary, is any data with state, that is attributes or a value, and defined behavior, that is methods (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A class is a template for creating user-defined objects, and the objects made from it are its instances. An attribute is a value associated with an object which is usually referenced by name using dotted expressions, so that an attribute a of an object o is written o.a. A method is a function which is defined inside a class body and which, called as an attribute of an instance, gets the instance as its first argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An object, in the words of the glossary, is any data with state, that is attributes or a value, and defined behavior, that is methods (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A class is a template for creating user-defined objects, and the objects made from it are its instances. An attribute is a value associated with an object which is usually referenced by name using dotted expressions, so that an attribute a of an object o is written o.a. A method is a function which is defined inside a class body and which, called as an attribute of an instance, gets the instance as its first argument (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The tools of this chapter are made of objects. An exception is an object that is created by calling a class, and it carries its message in an attribute. A logger, a handler and a log record are objects too, and the list method sort() that the chapter calls on its list of ages is a method of a list object (Sweigart, 2025). Sentences such as the exception stores its arguments in the attribute args, or call the logger's setLevel method, can be read only by a reader who knows what an attribute and a method are.

The executed checks show the vocabulary at work. The expression Exception('m') creates an instance, type(Exception('m')).__name__ is 'Exception', and isinstance(Exception('m'), Exception) is True. The attribute args of Exception('custom message') is the tuple ('custom message',). The string 'abc' is an object whose method upper, called as 'abc'.upper(), returns 'ABC', and hasattr(Exception('m'), 'add_note') is True, which says that an exception object has a method with that name.

The dotted name reaches into the object. After the dot comes either an attribute, which is a value, or a method, which is called by adding parentheses and arguments. The glossary's statement about the first argument can be checked: 'abc'.upper() and str.upper('abc') both return 'ABC', the second call passing the instance explicitly where the first passes it by the dot. A module is reached in the same way, which is why random.randint and logging.debug are written with a dot.

The parentheses decide what the expression means. args is a value, so Exception('m').args() raises a TypeError with the message 'tuple' object is not callable. And 'abc'.upper without parentheses is not an error, but it is not the result either: it is the method itself, whose text starts with <built-in method upper of str object. A call that appears to do nothing is often a method written without its parentheses.

nodes.definition: An object is data with state and behaviour; an attribute is a value reached from it by a dotted name, and a method is a function reached the same way and called with parentheses.

nodes.label: Command line
nodes.body: The command line is the line of text that a person types in a terminal to start a program. A terminal is the text window in which such lines are typed and their answers shown. The documentation gives the general shape of the line for Python: python, then options, then one of -c command, -m module-name, a script, or -, then arguments; and it names the most common use case as a simple invocation of a script, python myscript.py (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation adds that the interpreter scans the command line and the environment for various settings.

paras.text: The command line is the line of text that a person types in a terminal to start a program. A terminal is the text window in which such lines are typed and their answers shown. The documentation gives the general shape of the line for Python: python, then options, then one of -c command, -m module-name, a script, or -, then arguments; and it names the most common use case as a simple invocation of a script, python myscript.py (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation adds that the interpreter scans the command line and the environment for various settings.

Several tools of this chapter are controlled from the command line. The option -O switches assertions off, python -m pdb main.py runs a program under the debugger, python -m pdb -p followed by a process identifier attaches to a running program, and the setting PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 is placed in the environment of the command. An editor's Run and Debug buttons hide the command line, but the choices it expresses are still there, and a student who knows them can reproduce a run exactly.

The command line is met whenever a program is started outside an editor. In the executed check, the command python -c followed by import sys; print(sys.argv) and the two arguments a and b prints ['-c', 'a', 'b'], and a script saved as main.py and started with the same two arguments prints ['main.py', 'a', 'b']. The first item is the name that stands for the program, and the rest are the arguments, in the order typed.

The position of a word decides who reads it. Words before the script name or the -c command are options for Python itself. Words after them are arguments for the program, which reads them in sys.argv. Executed check: a script that prints sys.flags.optimize and sys.argv and is started as python main.py -O prints 0 and ['main.py', '-O'], so the -O reached the program and did not switch optimisation on.

A misplaced option is silently taken as an argument. python main.py -O does not run the program with assertions off, and in the executed check python -m pdb main.py -O hands -O to the program being debugged, which prints 0 ['main.py', '-O'], and not to Python. The documentation's own description of the interpreter's options is the place to check where an option belongs.

nodes.definition: The command line is the line of text typed in a terminal to start a program: the interpreter, then options, then what to run, then arguments for the program.

nodes.label: File and directory
nodes.body: A file is a named piece of data stored on the computer, which a program reads or writes through a file object. The tutorial explains that open() returns a file object and takes the filename as its first argument, a string, and a mode as its second (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The mode 'r' means that the file will only be read, 'w' means only writing, and 'a' opens the file for appending. A directory is a place that holds files, and the current working directory of a program is returned by os.getcwd() as a string (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The path of a file is the text that says in which directory it is.

paras.text: A file is a named piece of data stored on the computer, which a program reads or writes through a file object. The tutorial explains that open() returns a file object and takes the filename as its first argument, a string, and a mode as its second (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The mode 'r' means that the file will only be read, 'w' means only writing, and 'a' opens the file for appending. A directory is a place that holds files, and the current working directory of a program is returned by os.getcwd() as a string (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The path of a file is the text that says in which directory it is.

The logging branch writes to files, and several settings of the debugger and of the editors keep their data in files as well. A student has to know where a file is written and what writing it does to an older file with the same name. The tutorial states that mode 'w' erases an existing file with the same name, whereas 'a' adds to the end of it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A log that is written with 'w' every time keeps only the last run, and a log written with 'a' keeps every run.

In the chapter the file is the log file: logging.basicConfig(filename='myProgramLog.txt', ...) saves the log messages to that file instead of showing them on the screen (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed check a file is written with the mode 'w' twice, with the texts one and two, and then reads back as two only; after a write in mode 'a' of three, the file holds the two words two and three. The type of the open file is TextIOWrapper, the class of a text file object.

A file is used in three steps: open, read or write, close. The tutorial says that in text mode strings are read and written, encoded in a specific encoding, and recommends encoding='utf-8' unless a different one is needed (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The glossary explains that to store a string it has to be serialized as a sequence of bytes, and the text encoding is the rule for that. A name without a directory, such as 'workfile', is looked for in the current working directory, which the executed check confirms by finding os.getcwd() to be a directory.

The filename alone does not say where a file is. The same name in another directory is another file, so a program that is started from a different directory writes its log somewhere else. Opening an existing file for writing destroys its contents, as the mode 'w' does, and there is no undo. And a file that was not closed may not have its last data written; closing it, as the tutorial's examples do, makes sure that it has.

nodes.definition: A file is a named piece of stored data that a program can read and write; a directory holds files, and a path says where a file is.

nodes.label: Error signalling
nodes.body: Error signalling is the way a program says that something has gone wrong. In Python the saying is done with exceptions: an exception is an object that carries a description of the problem and travels up through the running code until something handles it. Python raises exceptions by itself whenever it tries to execute invalid code, and the programmer can raise them deliberately with the raise statement (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Error signalling is the way a program says that something has gone wrong. In Python the saying is done with exceptions: an exception is an object that carries a description of the problem and travels up through the running code until something handles it. Python raises exceptions by itself whenever it tries to execute invalid code, and the programmer can raise them deliberately with the raise statement (Sweigart, 2025).

A program that cannot say what went wrong cannot be repaired, either by its author or by its user. Signalling also separates two jobs that belong in different places: the code that notices a problem and the code that decides what to do about it. The chapter states the point plainly: it is often the code that calls a function, and not the function itself, that knows how to handle an exception (Sweigart, 2025).

Every Python program meets error signalling, usually first as a traceback printed on the screen after a crash. The chapter extends the earlier treatment of try and except, which handled exceptions that Python raised, with the other half of the story: raising exceptions on purpose and reading what an unhandled one prints (Sweigart, 2025).

This branch has two parts. The first, raising, shows how a function refuses a call it cannot serve, which class of exception to choose, how the message travels with the exception and what happens if nobody handles it. The second, tracebacks, explains the record that an exception leaves as it passes through the call stack, and how to read it, including the finer marks and the notes that recent versions of Python add.

nodes.label: Raising
nodes.body: Raising is the act of signalling an exception on purpose. The chapter's section Raising Exceptions explains that raising an exception is a way of saying: stop running this code, and move the program execution to the except statement (Sweigart, 2025). The code that raises does not know who will handle the problem, only that it cannot continue.

paras.text: Raising is the act of signalling an exception on purpose. The chapter's section Raising Exceptions explains that raising an exception is a way of saying: stop running this code, and move the program execution to the except statement (Sweigart, 2025). The code that raises does not know who will handle the problem, only that it cannot continue.

Raising turns a silent wrong answer into a loud, early failure. A function that is given an argument it cannot work with has only two honest choices, to return something misleading or to refuse, and raising is the refusal. The caller, which knows the larger context, can then recover, ask the user again or stop.

The concepts that follow describe the statement itself, the exception classes from which a raiser chooses, the message that is passed along, the use of raising to validate the arguments of a function, and the outcome when no handler exists.

The statement, the class and the message are three separate choices, and each can be read back afterwards. The statement stops the function at once and hands the exception upward; the class is what a handler names, so a ValueError is caught by except ValueError and passes straight through except TypeError; and the message travels inside the object, where str of the exception gives the text and its args attribute gives the tuple it was built from (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A raise that meets no handler anywhere ends the program with a traceback and an exit status of 1, so the failure is visible to whatever started it.

nodes.label: Raise statement
nodes.body: A raise statement signals an exception on purpose. In the chapter it consists of the keyword raise, a call to Exception, and a string with a helpful error message passed to that call (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference gives the general rule: raise evaluates its expression and the result must be a subclass or an instance of BaseException, the base of all exceptions; if it is a class, an instance is created by calling the class with no arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A raise statement signals an exception on purpose. In the chapter it consists of the keyword raise, a call to Exception, and a string with a helpful error message passed to that call (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference gives the general rule: raise evaluates its expression and the result must be a subclass or an instance of BaseException, the base of all exceptions; if it is a class, an instance is created by calling the class with no arguments (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The statement lets a function enforce its own requirements. The chapter's function box_print draws a box from a character, a width and a height, and it raises an exception when the symbol is not one character long or when the width or the height is not greater than 2. Without those checks the function would draw a meaningless shape or fail later in a way that is harder to trace (Sweigart, 2025).

A raise statement is typically written inside a function, and the try and except statements that handle the exception are written in the code that calls the function. When the chapter's program calls box_print('x', 1, 3) inside a try block, the exception raised for the width is caught by the except clause and the program prints An exception happened: Width must be greater than 2. A second call with the two-character symbol ZZ prints An exception happened: Symbol must be a single character string. (Sweigart, 2025).

When Python executes raise, it stops the current function at that line and starts looking for an except clause that matches the exception, first in the function itself and then in each caller above it. A bare raise with no expression inside an except clause re-raises the exception that is being handled, so a handler can look at an error and then let it continue (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The statement raise ValueError is shorthand for raise ValueError(), which creates the exception without a message.

A raise statement outside any try block does not give an error of its own; it ends the program with a traceback. And a raise inside a function does not return a value to the caller: the code after it in the same function never runs. Write the message so that someone who has not seen the code can act on it; Width must be greater than 2. says what was wrong and what is needed.

nodes.definition: A raise statement stops the running code and passes an exception to the nearest matching except clause, which is how a function tells its caller that a call was invalid.

nodes.label: Exception class
nodes.body: An exception class is the kind of an exception, and each kind is a class. A class is a pattern from which objects are made, and a subclass is a class that inherits from another and so counts as a kind of that other class. Python's built-in exceptions form a hierarchy with BaseException at the top, and Exception, from which all built-in exceptions that do not exit the interpreter are derived, directly beneath it (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An exception class is the kind of an exception, and each kind is a class. A class is a pattern from which objects are made, and a subclass is a class that inherits from another and so counts as a kind of that other class. Python's built-in exceptions form a hierarchy with BaseException at the top, and Exception, from which all built-in exceptions that do not exit the interpreter are derived, directly beneath it (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The class tells a handler what happened without parsing the message. ValueError is documented as raised when an operation or function receives an argument that has the right type but an inappropriate value; TypeError, NameError and ZeroDivisionError each name a different situation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that raises the most specific class lets its callers write except clauses that react to one problem and leave the others alone.

The class name is the first word on the last line of every traceback, for example ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'. The chapter raises plain Exception objects with a message, which is the simplest form; the tutorial advises that programs that define their own exceptions derive them from the Exception class and give them names that end in Error (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

An except clause names a class and catches every exception that is an instance of that class or of a subclass. The expression issubclass(ValueError, Exception) is True, so except Exception catches a ValueError, whereas except TypeError does not: a program that raises ValueError('bad value') inside a try block with only an except TypeError clause is not stopped there, and the exception is caught by an outer except ValueError clause that prints outer caught bad value.

Catching Exception is the broadest ordinary choice and hides the difference between a mistake by the user and a mistake by the programmer, so prefer the narrowest class that fits. The most extreme classes, such as KeyboardInterrupt, are not subclasses of Exception: issubclass(KeyboardInterrupt, Exception) is False, so an except Exception clause does not catch a user's Control-C.

nodes.definition: The kind of an exception: ValueError, TypeError and the others are classes derived from Exception, and an except clause catches the classes it names.

error.out: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'

nodes.label: Exception message
nodes.body: The message of an exception is the text that was passed to it when it was created. The exception stores its arguments in the attribute args, which is a tuple, a fixed sequence of values, and calling str on the exception returns the arguments as text, or the empty string if there were none (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the chapter the message is the string passed to Exception(), for example Width must be greater than 2.

paras.text: The message of an exception is the text that was passed to it when it was created. The exception stores its arguments in the attribute args, which is a tuple, a fixed sequence of values, and calling str on the exception returns the arguments as text, or the empty string if there were none (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the chapter the message is the string passed to Exception(), for example Width must be greater than 2.

The message is the part of an error that a person reads. A program that prints a clear message when something goes wrong helps the user to correct the input, whereas a traceback shows only the programmer where the code was. The chapter uses the except Exception as err form for exactly this purpose: it stores the exception object in a variable named err and converts it to a string with str to produce a user-friendly error message (Sweigart, 2025).

The form appears in the chapter's boxPrint.py: the except clause prints the text An exception happened: followed by str(err). The same form is the standard way to show or log an error without letting the program crash, and the message is the line that follows the class name in a traceback (Sweigart, 2025).

Writing as err after the class in the except clause binds the exception that was caught to the name err for the length of the clause. The expression Exception('custom message').args evaluates to ('custom message',), a tuple with one item, and str(Exception('custom message')) evaluates to 'custom message'. An exception with two arguments is shown as a tuple, str(Exception('a', 'b')) being '('a', 'b')', and an exception created without arguments has an empty message.

The message is for people and not for code. A handler that decides what to do by comparing the text of the message breaks as soon as the wording changes, so decide by the exception class and keep the message for display. Printing the exception object directly, print(err), shows the same text as print(str(err)), because print converts its arguments to strings (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: The text passed to an exception is kept in its args and printed by str, so an except clause can show a message written for the user instead of a traceback.

nodes.label: Argument validation
nodes.body: Argument validation is the practice of checking the values a function receives before the function uses them, and raising an exception when they cannot be used. The chapter's function box_print validates its three arguments with if statements, one for the length of the symbol and two for the size, and each failed test is followed by a raise statement with a message (Sweigart, 2025). A condition, an expression that evaluates to True or False, decides whether the exception is raised.

paras.text: Argument validation is the practice of checking the values a function receives before the function uses them, and raising an exception when they cannot be used. The chapter's function box_print validates its three arguments with if statements, one for the length of the symbol and two for the size, and each failed test is followed by a raise statement with a message (Sweigart, 2025). A condition, an expression that evaluates to True or False, decides whether the exception is raised.

A function cannot trust its callers, and a user who typed something into a program is the least trustworthy caller of all. Validating at the start of the function keeps a bad value from travelling deeper into the program, where it would cause a failure far from its source. The chapter says that for errors a program can meet as a normal part of its operation, such as a file not being found or invalid data entered by the user, an exception should be raised and not detected with an assert statement (Sweigart, 2025).

Validation is found at the top of almost every function that receives data from outside: a user, a file or another program. The Python glossary names two coding styles around this idea. Look before you leap tests the preconditions with if statements before acting; easier to ask for forgiveness than permission assumes that things are valid and catches the exception if not (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Validation with raise is the first style, and the try and except around a call is the second.

A small function shows the pattern. After def area(width), the lines if width <= 0 and raise ValueError('width must be positive, got ' + str(width)) refuse the bad value before the function computes width * 2. A loop that calls area(3) and area(0) inside try prints 6 for the first call and refused: width must be positive, got 0 for the second.

Do the validation before any effect of the function has happened, such as printing or changing data, so that a refused call leaves nothing half done. Put in the message the value that was received and the value that was expected. And do not validate with assert: an assert statement can be removed from a running program, and a check that must always happen belongs in an if with a raise.

nodes.definition: Checking the arguments a function receives before using them and raising an exception that names the problem when they are unusable.

nodes.label: Unhandled exception
nodes.body: An unhandled exception is one that no except clause matches. The chapter describes the consequence in one sentence: if no try and except statements cover the raise statement that raised the exception, the program simply crashes and displays the exception's error message (Sweigart, 2025). Crashing here means that Python stops running the program at that point.

paras.text: An unhandled exception is one that no except clause matches. The chapter describes the consequence in one sentence: if no try and except statements cover the raise statement that raised the exception, the program simply crashes and displays the exception's error message (Sweigart, 2025). Crashing here means that Python stops running the program at that point.

Letting an exception go unhandled is often the right design. A programming error that the program cannot repair is better reported at once, with the traceback that shows its origin, than hidden. The Python tutorial observes that most exceptions are not handled by programs and result in error messages (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The situation is met whenever a program fails with a traceback in the terminal, and it is the usual fate of an AssertionError, which the chapter says should not be caught. The interpreter's hook for it is sys.excepthook: when an exception other than SystemExit is raised and uncaught, the interpreter calls this function with the exception class, the exception instance and the traceback, and it prints them to sys.stderr (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A program that prints before, raises Exception('boom') and then has a print of after shows exactly the behaviour. Only before reaches the screen, the traceback ends with the line Exception: boom, and the process finishes with the exit status 1. The statement after the raise never runs. Shells and other programs treat a nonzero exit status as abnormal termination (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A crash can leave work unfinished, such as a half-written result, so a program that must clean up needs a finally clause or a handler near the top. In the other direction, do not wrap the whole program in except Exception only to hide tracebacks: the traceback is the most useful clue that the program has.

nodes.definition: An exception that no except clause matches ends the program: Python prints a traceback on the error stream and the process finishes with a nonzero exit status.

nodes.label: Tracebacks
nodes.body: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an exception is not handled. It lists the chain of function calls that led to the line where the exception was raised, ending with the class and the message of the exception. The Python tutorial calls the preceding part of the error message the context in which the exception occurred, in the form of a stack traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A traceback is the report that Python prints when an exception is not handled. It lists the chain of function calls that led to the line where the exception was raised, ending with the class and the message of the exception. The Python tutorial calls the preceding part of the error message the context in which the exception occurred, in the form of a stack traceback (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The traceback answers the question where the program was when it failed, and it answers it without running anything again. Reading it well is the most economical debugging skill: a learner who can read a traceback knows which file, which line and which call to look at first.

The concepts that follow explain how an exception travels up the call stack, how the lines of a traceback are read, how Python 3.11 and later point at the failing part of a line, how notes add context while an exception is re-raised, and why the report appears on the error stream.

The report says in its own first line how it should be read: Traceback (most recent call last) means that the failing line is the last one listed while the outermost call is at the top (Python Software Foundation, 2026). From Python 3.11 onwards the report also underlines the part of the line that failed, so a line chaining several calls shows which of them raised. The whole report goes to the error stream rather than the ordinary output stream, which is why sending a program's output to a file still leaves the traceback on the screen, and why the lines printed before the failure and the failure itself can be separated.

nodes.label: Exception unwinding
nodes.body: Exception unwinding is the way an exception travels from the place where it was raised back through the functions that were called to get there. The call stack is the list of functions that are currently running, the newest on top. An exception that a function does not handle leaves that function and arrives in the caller, and the process is repeated until an except clause matches the exception or the stack is empty.

paras.text: Exception unwinding is the way an exception travels from the place where it was raised back through the functions that were called to get there. The call stack is the list of functions that are currently running, the newest on top. An exception that a function does not handle leaves that function and arrives in the caller, and the process is repeated until an except clause matches the exception or the stack is empty.

Unwinding is what makes it possible to raise an exception in a deep helper function and handle it at the one place that knows what to do. The traceback is a record of the same journey, so understanding the unwinding is what makes a traceback readable: its lines are the functions that the exception left.

A program with three small functions shows it. In it process calls load, load calls read_age, and read_age calls int on its text. Given the text 'abc', int raises a ValueError in read_age, no function on the way handles it, and it is caught by an except ValueError clause around the call to process in the main program, which prints caught: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'.

The journey can be inspected, because the exception object keeps its traceback in its __traceback__ attribute (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Listing the function names of the traceback gives ['<module>', 'process', 'load', 'read_age'], from the outermost call to the one that raised. Without the handler, the same journey ends at the top of the program: Python prints the traceback, with these four entries, and the program ends with an exit status of 1.

The handler can be anywhere along the way, and the nearer it is to the raise the less of the program is skipped. A handler placed too low may swallow an error that a caller wanted to see, while one placed too high may skip work that could have been done. Decide where the program can do something useful about the error, and handle it there.

nodes.definition: An exception that no function handles leaves each function in turn, up the call stack, until an except clause matches it or the program ends with a traceback.

nodes.label: Traceback reading
nodes.body: Reading a traceback means taking its lines in order and understanding what each one says. The first line is the header Traceback (most recent call last):. Each following entry gives a file name, a line number and the name of the function in which a call was made, and under it the text of that line of source. The last line names the class and the message of the exception (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Reading a traceback means taking its lines in order and understanding what each one says. The first line is the header Traceback (most recent call last):. Each following entry gives a file name, a line number and the name of the function in which a call was made, and under it the text of that line of source. The last line names the class and the message of the exception (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The header says how the entries are arranged: the most recent call is last. The outermost call, usually the module itself, comes first, and the call that raised the exception comes last, just above the message. Because the cause of the exception is in the last entry and the reason it was reached is in the earlier ones, the reader usually starts at the bottom and works upwards.

In the three-function program of the previous concept, a traceback of the unhandled error begins with the header, continues with the entry File 'main.py', line 7, in <module>, and ends with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'. The names of the entries are <module>, process, load and read_age, with the line numbers 7, 6, 4 and 2, and the source line of the last entry is return int(text).

The line number is where execution was inside that function when it called the next one, so each entry except the last points at a call. The last entry points at the line that raised. The header and the last line are the same in every recent version of Python, but the lines between them are refined from release to release, for example by the finer marks that the next concept describes.

Reading from the top and stopping at the first entry is a common mistake. That entry is usually the main program calling something, and it is the last entry that shows where the problem happened. Note too that code typed directly into the interpreter or given with python -c has no file to read from, so such entries have no source line.

nodes.definition: A traceback lists the calls from the outermost to the one that raised, each with file, line, function and source line, and ends with the exception class and message.

nodes.label: Fine grained locations
nodes.body: Fine grained locations are the marks that a traceback draws under a line of source to show which part of it failed. A row of carets, ^, marks the failing operation, and a row of tildes, ~, runs under the part of the expression that it was applied to. The feature was proposed in PEP 657 and arrived in Python 3.11 (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021).

paras.text: Fine grained locations are the marks that a traceback draws under a line of source to show which part of it failed. A row of carets, ^, marks the failing operation, and a row of tildes, ~, runs under the part of the expression that it was applied to. The feature was proposed in PEP 657 and arrived in Python 3.11 (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021).

A single line can contain many operations. The PEP gives the case of x['a']['b']['c']['d'] = 1, where a TypeError that says 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable cannot tell which of the dictionaries was None, so users often had to attach a debugger or split up the expression (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). The marks answer the question directly.

The marks appear in any traceback printed by the standard interpreter. A dictionary maps keys to values, and a subscript is the square-bracket lookup of a key. For data = {'a': {'b': None}}, the line print(data['a']['b']['c']) fails with TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, and the carets lie under the last subscript, ['c'], while tildes run under data['a']['b'], the value that was None.

Python records, for each bytecode instruction, the start and end columns of the source it came from, and the traceback machinery uses these ranges to draw the marks (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). The marks depend on the interpreter: for the call line process('abc') of the previous concept, Python 3.14 draws tildes and carets and Python 3.12 does not, so the exact picture varies between versions even when the first and last lines are the same.

The marks can be switched off. The PEP provides the environment variable PYTHONNODEBUGRANGES and the option -X no_debug_ranges for those who want smaller files or a traceback in the old form (Galindo Salgado et al., 2021). A program that parses traceback text should therefore not rely on the marks being present.

nodes.definition: Since Python 3.11 a traceback marks the failing part of a line, so which subscript or call failed in a chained expression can be read from it.

nodes.label: Exception notes
nodes.body: An exception note is a short piece of text added to an exception after it has been created. The method add_note(note) adds a string to the exception's notes, which are kept in the list __notes__, and the standard traceback shows the notes after the exception string (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The feature was proposed in PEP 678 and arrived in Python 3.11 (Hatfield-Dodds, 2021).

paras.text: An exception note is a short piece of text added to an exception after it has been created. The method add_note(note) adds a string to the exception's notes, which are kept in the list __notes__, and the standard traceback shows the notes after the exception string (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The feature was proposed in PEP 678 and arrived in Python 3.11 (Hatfield-Dodds, 2021).

A message is written where the exception is raised, but the useful context is often known only further up, for example which record or which field was being processed. Notes allow the code that catches the exception to add this information and re-raise the same exception, without hiding the original class or traceback behind a new exception.

The pattern is used when a handler cannot repair a problem but knows more than the raiser. The Python tutorial shows a handler that adds a note and then uses a bare raise, so the traceback ends with the exception and its notes in the order they were added (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In a program that tries int('abc'), catches the ValueError, calls add_note('while reading the age field') and then raises again, the last two lines of the traceback are ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc' and while reading the age field. The attribute __notes__ is created when add_note is first called, and the example panel of this page uses a one-line unnamed function, called a lambda, only to fit the call and the reading of __notes__ into one expression.

The argument must be a string; passing anything else raises TypeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Notes are not part of the message, so str(err) does not contain them, and code that logs only str(err) loses them. Notes do not exist in versions before 3.11, so a program that must run on an older interpreter cannot call add_note.

nodes.definition: An exception can carry notes added with add_note, kept in __notes__ and printed after the traceback, so code that re-raises can add context.

nodes.label: Standard error stream
nodes.body: The standard error stream is a second channel of output that every program has next to its ordinary output. Python's documentation describes the standard streams as file objects: stdin is used for all interactive input, including calls to input; stdout is used for the output of print and for the prompts of input; and the interpreter's own prompts and error messages go to stderr (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A stream is simply a flow of text out of or into the program.

paras.text: The standard error stream is a second channel of output that every program has next to its ordinary output. Python's documentation describes the standard streams as file objects: stdin is used for all interactive input, including calls to input; stdout is used for the output of print and for the prompts of input; and the interpreter's own prompts and error messages go to stderr (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A stream is simply a flow of text out of or into the program.

Two channels let a program separate its results from its complaints. The results can be saved or passed on to another program while the error messages remain visible to the person at the terminal. A traceback is therefore never mixed into the normal output.

In a terminal both streams are shown on the same screen, so the difference is easy to miss, but a program that captures the output of another sees it. In a test where a program prints one line normally and one line with print(..., file=sys.stderr), the standard output holds only to stdout and the standard error holds only to stderr. The standard logging handler also writes to sys.stderr when no other stream is given (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The function print writes to sys.stdout unless the keyword argument file is given, and an uncaught exception is reported by sys.excepthook, which prints the traceback to sys.stderr (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Writing to the error stream on purpose therefore needs only print(..., file=sys.stderr), where sys is the module that holds the streams.

Do not print the information that other programs must read to the error stream, and do not print error messages to the standard output of a program whose output is processed further. Remember, too, that a log message sent to the screen goes by default to the error stream, not to the standard output.

nodes.definition: The second output channel of a program, used by the interpreter for tracebacks and error messages, separate from the standard output that print uses.

nodes.label: Assertion
nodes.body: An assertion is a statement that a certain condition must be true at a certain point of a program, together with a check that stops the program at once if it is not. The chapter calls an assertion a sanity check, a test that makes sure the code is not doing something obviously wrong, and it performs such checks with the assert statement, which raises an AssertionError exception when the check fails (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: An assertion is a statement that a certain condition must be true at a certain point of a program, together with a check that stops the program at once if it is not. The chapter calls an assertion a sanity check, a test that makes sure the code is not doing something obviously wrong, and it performs such checks with the assert statement, which raises an AssertionError exception when the check fails (Sweigart, 2025).

Assertions catch bugs close to their cause. The chapter recommends failing fast: a program that stops the moment a necessary condition is violated shortens the time between the original cause of the bug and the moment the programmer first notices it, and so reduces the amount of code to check (Sweigart, 2025). A wrong value that is allowed to travel through the program causes a failure far from its source.

Assertions are written by the programmer, for the programmer. They appear at the boundaries inside a program: after a computation whose result has a known property, before using a value that earlier code was supposed to prepare, and at the end of a function whose contract can be stated in a line. The chapter limits them to programmer errors and keeps user errors for exceptions (Sweigart, 2025).

This branch explains the assert statement with its form, its optional message and its failure, then the check that the chapter uses as its example, the difference between assertions and raised exceptions, and finally the optimised mode in which Python removes assertions altogether, which is the chapter's rule restated as a fact about the interpreter.

nodes.label: Assert
nodes.body: The assert group covers the mechanics and the discipline of assertions. The mechanics are the statement, the check it performs, the error it raises and the message it can carry. The discipline is the knowledge of what an assertion may check and what it must not.

paras.text: The assert group covers the mechanics and the discipline of assertions. The mechanics are the statement, the check it performs, the error it raises and the message it can carry. The discipline is the knowledge of what an assertion may check and what it must not.

Assertions are easy to write and easy to misuse. The same statement that gives an early warning during development can become a security or correctness hole if it stands in for a check that must always run, because Python can be told to leave assertions out. The concepts of this group therefore pair every mechanism with the limit that goes with it.

The concepts begin with the idea of the sanity check and the statement that implements it, then the list example from the chapter, the failure, the message, the rule of fail fast, the choice between assertion and exception, the option that removes assertions, and the command-line options in general.

The mechanism and its limit are each one line away. The statement assert 1 == 2, 'numbers differ' raises AssertionError: numbers differ and ends the program with an exit status of 1, while the same file run as python -O prints its last line and ends with a status of 0, because that option removes every assertion from the compiled code (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That is the whole of the discipline: an assertion may state what the programmer believes can never happen, and it may never be the only check standing between a program and input it cannot trust.

nodes.label: Sanity check
nodes.body: A sanity check is a quick test that a result is not obviously wrong. It does not prove that a program is correct; it checks a property that must hold if the preceding code did its job, and it fails loudly when the property is violated. The chapter defines an assertion in just these terms: a sanity check to make sure the code is not doing something obviously wrong (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A sanity check is a quick test that a result is not obviously wrong. It does not prove that a program is correct; it checks a property that must hold if the preceding code did its job, and it fails loudly when the property is violated. The chapter defines an assertion in just these terms: a sanity check to make sure the code is not doing something obviously wrong (Sweigart, 2025).

The value of a sanity check lies in its cost and its timing. It costs one line and little running time, and it runs at the very point where the assumption is made, so a violation is reported there and not three functions later. The chapter's own example checks that after a list has been sorted its first item is not larger than its last (Sweigart, 2025).

Typical sanity checks compare a computed total with the sum of its parts, check that a result has the expected length, check that a number lies within its allowed range, or check that a collection that should be sorted is in order. They are placed directly after the code whose result they test.

The check is a condition, an expression whose value is True or False, and the assert statement stops the program when it is false. For example, sorted([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3] evaluates to True, so the check passes in silence, whereas sorted([3, 1, 2]) == [3, 2, 1] evaluates to False and an assertion built from it would fail.

A sanity check should be independent of the code it checks. If it recomputes the result with the same faulty logic, it will agree with the bug. And a check that is wrong itself, for example a comparison with the wrong operator, produces false alarms that teach the programmer to ignore assertions.

nodes.definition: A cheap test of a result that must hold if the code before it is correct, written to catch an obvious mistake early.

nodes.label: Assert statement
nodes.body: The assert statement checks a condition and raises an AssertionError exception if the condition is false. In the chapter it consists of the keyword assert, a condition that is an expression evaluating to True or False, and optionally a comma followed by a string to display when the condition is False (Sweigart, 2025). In plain English it says: I assert that the condition holds, and if not, there is a bug somewhere, so stop the program immediately.

paras.text: The assert statement checks a condition and raises an AssertionError exception if the condition is false. In the chapter it consists of the keyword assert, a condition that is an expression evaluating to True or False, and optionally a comma followed by a string to display when the condition is False (Sweigart, 2025). In plain English it says: I assert that the condition holds, and if not, there is a bug somewhere, so stop the program immediately.

The statement turns a belief into a check. A programmer who writes assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] records a belief about the list, and the interpreter verifies it every time the line runs. If the belief becomes false, because of a later change or an input that was not foreseen, the statement reports it at once.

The statement is used in programs, in functions, and in the interactive shell, as the chapter does when it enters assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] after sorting a list (Sweigart, 2025). The Python language reference introduces assert statements as a convenient way to insert debugging assertions into a program (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The language reference defines the simple form, assert expression, as equivalent to if __debug__: followed by if not expression: raise AssertionError, and the form with a message as the same with raise AssertionError(expression2) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The special name __debug__ is normally True, so the check runs. When the condition is true the statement does nothing at all, and the program continues with the next line.

Do not put the condition and the message in parentheses together. The statement assert (False, 'msg') tests a tuple with two items, and a tuple that is not empty counts as true, so the check can never fail; Python warns about it with a SyntaxWarning that says assertion is always true, perhaps remove parentheses? (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Also avoid conditions that change something, because under optimisation the condition is not evaluated at all.

nodes.definition: An assert statement checks a condition the programmer believes is true and raises AssertionError when it is false.

nodes.label: Sorted-order check
nodes.body: The sorted-order check is the chapter's example of an assertion. It uses a list, which is an ordered collection of values written between square brackets, such as [26, 57, 92]. Items are reached by their position, called the index, which starts at 0, so ages[0] is the first item, and a negative index counts from the end, so ages[-1] is the last item (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The sorted-order check is the chapter's example of an assertion. It uses a list, which is an ordered collection of values written between square brackets, such as [26, 57, 92]. Items are reached by their position, called the index, which starts at 0, so ages[0] is the first item, and a negative index counts from the end, so ages[-1] is the last item (Sweigart, 2025).

The example shows how a single assert guards a whole step of work. If the list has really been sorted from smallest to largest, then the first item cannot be larger than the last. If the check fails, something other than sorting has happened to the list, which is the kind of bug that would otherwise show up much later as a strange result.

In the chapter the list is ages = [26, 57, 92, 54, 22, 15, 17, 80, 47, 73]. The method sort() puts the items in ascending order in place, giving [15, 17, 22, 26, 47, 54, 57, 73, 80, 92], and the assertion passes. The method reverse() reverses the list in place, giving [73, 47, 80, 17, 15, 22, 54, 92, 57, 26], and the same assertion raises an AssertionError (Sweigart, 2025).

Both sort() and reverse() change the list in place, which is why the chapter calls them in separate statements and then looks at the list (Python Software Foundation, 2026); when they are run they give back None, so a line such as ages = ages.sort() would destroy the list. The comparison ages[0] <= ages[-1] is True for the sorted list, because 15 <= 92, and False for the reversed one, because 73 <= 26 is false. The example panel of this page uses a one-line unnamed function, a lambda, only to sort a list and compare in one expression.

The check is deliberately weak. A list in which the first item happens to be smaller than the last passes the assertion even though the list is not sorted, as [1, 3, 2] does. A stronger check compares every neighbouring pair, or compares the list with sorted(list). Choose a check strong enough for the risk, and remember that it protects only against the mistake it names.

nodes.definition: The chapter's example of a sanity check on a list: after sort() the first item is not larger than the last, and after reverse() it is.

nodes.label: Assertion failure
nodes.body: An assertion failure is the event in which an assert statement finds its condition false and raises AssertionError.
