The built-in exceptions page describes the class in one line: raised when an assert statement fails (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is an ordinary exception, a subclass of Exception, and so it travels up the call stack like any other.

paras.text: An assertion failure is the event in which an assert statement finds its condition false and raises AssertionError. The built-in exceptions page describes the class in one line: raised when an assert statement fails (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It is an ordinary exception, a subclass of Exception, and so it travels up the call stack like any other.

What distinguishes it is how the chapter wants it treated. Unlike other exceptions, assert statements should not be handled with try and except; if an assert fails, the program should crash (Sweigart, 2025). The failure means that the programmer's model of the program is wrong, and a handler that continues with a wrong model only postpones the damage.

A failure shows up as a traceback whose last line is AssertionError, followed by the message if the assert had one. In the chapter's example the line assert ages[0] <= ages[-1] fails on the reversed list, and the traceback ends with AssertionError and nothing after it, because no message was given (Sweigart, 2025). In current Python the traceback also marks the whole condition under the failing line.

Because no message was given, the exception's text is empty: str(AssertionError()) is the empty string. Because the class derives from Exception, issubclass(AssertionError, Exception) evaluates to True, so an except Exception clause would catch it, and that is exactly what the advice warns against. An unhandled failure ends the program with exit status 1, like any other unhandled exception.

Never catch AssertionError to keep a program going. If a check is needed for input that comes from outside the program, the right tool is an if statement that raises a more specific exception such as ValueError, which a caller can reasonably handle.

nodes.definition: A failed assertion is an ordinary exception of class AssertionError; the chapter advises against catching it, since it reports a programmer error.

nodes.label: Assert message
nodes.body: The assert message is the optional second part of an assert statement. After the condition comes a comma and an expression, usually a string, and if the condition is false the value of that expression becomes the message of the AssertionError. The chapter lists it as the string to display when the condition is False (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The assert message is the optional second part of an assert statement. After the condition comes a comma and an expression, usually a string, and if the condition is false the value of that expression becomes the message of the AssertionError. The chapter lists it as the string to display when the condition is False (Sweigart, 2025).

A message tells the reader what the failed condition meant in the vocabulary of the program. The language reference remarks that it is unnecessary to include the source code of the failed expression in the message, since it is displayed as part of the stack trace, so the message is best used for the values that the source cannot show (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A message is useful when the same assertion could fail for several reasons or when the values matter. A common form builds the message with an f-string, for example assert x > 0, f'x must be positive, got {x}', which for x equal to -1 gives the message x must be positive, got -1.

The second expression is evaluated only when the condition is false (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A function that prints msg evaluated before returning the text bad and is used as the message does not run when the condition is true, and the program continues; when the condition is false it runs once and the error text is bad. This is why a message can safely contain a call that would be wasteful to execute on every pass.

Keep the message free of side effects, since it runs only on failure and would make the failing run behave differently from a passing one. And keep it short and factual: the text goes to the programmer, not to the user, and a user should never see it.

nodes.example: assert x > 0, f'x must be positive, got {x}'
nodes.definition: An assert statement can carry a second expression, evaluated only on failure, whose text becomes the message of the AssertionError.

nodes.label: Fail fast
nodes.body: Failing fast is the principle of stopping a program at the first sign that something is wrong. The chapter uses the phrase for assertions: by failing fast like this, the time between the original cause of the bug and the moment of first noticing it is shortened, and so is the amount of code that has to be checked to find the cause (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Failing fast is the principle of stopping a program at the first sign that something is wrong. The chapter uses the phrase for assertions: by failing fast like this, the time between the original cause of the bug and the moment of first noticing it is shortened, and so is the amount of code that has to be checked to find the cause (Sweigart, 2025).

The distance between cause and symptom is what makes bugs expensive. A negative value that enters a calculation may produce a wrong total that is printed pages later. If the program had stopped at the negative value, the cause would have been on the line in the traceback.

The principle is applied wherever a check can be placed cheaply near the assumption: at the start of a function, after an input has been converted, and after a step whose result is known to have a property. The chapter summarises that assertions are only for errors the program should not try to recover from, and that they should fail fast; otherwise an exception should be raised (Sweigart, 2025).

A program that does not fail fast continues to run with bad data, and the damage grows with every step. A program that does fail fast raises the exception at once, Python prints a traceback that names the file and line of the check, and the search for the cause starts there. The assert statement is the simplest implementation of the idea, and the raise statement is the more general one.

Failing fast belongs in development and in code where an error is a bug. For a service that must keep running or a program with a user at the keyboard, the same moment of detection should lead to a handled exception or a clear message, and not to a crash that destroys the user's work.

nodes.example: assert at the point of the assumption
nodes.definition: Stopping a program as soon as a necessary condition is violated, so that the failure appears near its cause.

nodes.label: Assert versus raise
nodes.body: Assert and raise are two ways of stopping a program that has met a bad condition, and the chapter assigns each a different kind of error. Assertions are for programmer errors, not user errors. Errors that a program can meet as a normal part of its operation, such as a file that is not found or invalid data typed by the user, are handled by raising an exception (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Assert and raise are two ways of stopping a program that has met a bad condition, and the chapter assigns each a different kind of error. Assertions are for programmer errors, not user errors. Errors that a program can meet as a normal part of its operation, such as a file that is not found or invalid data typed by the user, are handled by raising an exception (Sweigart, 2025).

The difference matters because the two have different audiences and different guarantees. An exception is part of the program's behaviour and the user may see its message. An assertion should fail only while the program is under development, and a user should never see an assertion error in a finished program (Sweigart, 2025). The language reference adds a technical difference: assert is equivalent to raising AssertionError only when __debug__ is true, so an assertion may not run at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A function that sets an age shows the choice. If the age comes from a form that a person filled in, a negative value is a user error, and the function checks it with if age < 0 and raises ValueError. If the age was computed by earlier code that is supposed to return only non-negative values, a negative age means that the program itself is wrong, and an assert age >= 0 expresses that belief.

A practical test is to ask who could cause the condition to be false. If a user, a file, a network or another program could, then the check must always run and must lead to a recoverable error, so it is an if with a raise. If only a mistake in the program itself could, then it is an assertion. Because assertions can be removed by an option of the interpreter, only the second kind may rely on them.

The boundary moves. A function that is called only from the program's own code may use an assertion for its argument, and the same function offered to other programmers as a library must validate its arguments with exceptions, because strangers do not follow the program's own rules.

nodes.definition: An error the user can cause is checked with an if and a raise; an assert states what must be true if the program is correct.

nodes.label: Optimised mode
nodes.body: Optimised mode is a way of running Python in which assert statements are removed. The command-line option -O removes assert statements and any code that is conditional on the value of __debug__ (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in constant __debug__ is true if Python was not started with -O (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Optimised mode is a way of running Python in which assert statements are removed. The command-line option -O removes assert statements and any code that is conditional on the value of __debug__ (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in constant __debug__ is true if Python was not started with -O (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The mode explains the chapter's rule that assertions are for programmer errors. A program that depends on an assertion for correct behaviour would behave differently when run with -O, so assertions must never carry a check that the program needs for its own safety, such as validation of what a user typed.

The mode is met when a program is run with optimisation in real use, when the environment variable PYTHONOPTIMIZE is set, and when code is compiled by hand. The function compile takes an optimize level in which 0 means no optimisation and __debug__ is true, 1 means that asserts are removed and __debug__ is false, and 2 removes docstrings too, that is the string literals that appear as the first expression of a function, class or module (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The statement assert False normally raises AssertionError. A program that runs assert False and then prints reached prints nothing on the screen but a traceback in a normal run, and prints reached when it is started with python -O. In the same way __debug__ is True in a normal run and False under -O, and compiling a source string with optimize=1 and executing it reaches the line after the assert.

The compiler, the part of Python that turns source code into bytecode, emits no code for an assert statement when optimisation is requested, so even a condition with a side effect is not evaluated (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Test a program that is meant to run with -O under that option as well. Assignments to __debug__ are illegal, so a program cannot switch its assertions on or off by itself.

nodes.definition: Under the -O option, and in code compiled with optimisation, assert statements produce no code at all, so a check that must always run is not written as an assertion.

nodes.label: Command-line option
nodes.body: A command-line option is a word that begins with a hyphen and is written after the name of the interpreter to change how it runs, as in python -O script.py. The documentation gives the general form python [-bBdEhiIOPqRsSuvVWx?] [-c command | -m module-name | script | - ] [args], and says that the most common use is simply python myscript.py (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A command-line option is a word that begins with a hyphen and is written after the name of the interpreter to change how it runs, as in python -O script.py. The documentation gives the general form python [-bBdEhiIOPqRsSuvVWx?] [-c command | -m module-name | script | - ] [args], and says that the most common use is simply python myscript.py (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Options let one installation of Python behave in several ways without changing any program. This chapter uses three of them: -O, which removes assertions, -c, which runs the statements given on the command line, and -m, which runs a module as a script, as in python -m pdb. A learner who knows the options can read the documentation of the interpreter and of the tools that go with it.

Options are typed in a terminal after the name of the interpreter. A running program can find out which of them are in force: the value sys.flags reports them, and its optimize field stands for -O or -OO, so it is 0 in a normal run and 1 under -O (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The interpreter reads the options first and then the program. An interface option such as -c or -m ends the list of options that the interpreter itself consumes, and the arguments after it end up in sys.argv, where the program or the module run with -m reads them (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That is why, in python -m pdb -p, the -p belongs to the debugger and not to the interpreter. For example, python -O -c 'print(__debug__)' prints False, and python -c 'print(__debug__)' prints True.

Options and environment variables overlap: the documentation notes that it is customary for command-line switches to override environment variables where there is a conflict (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Because several versions of Python may be installed side by side, check which interpreter and which options a script is actually run with when its behaviour surprises you.

nodes.definition: A flag written after the python command, such as -O, -c, -m or -V, that changes how the interpreter runs.

nodes.label: Logging
nodes.body: Logging is the practice of making a program write down what it does while it runs. The Python logging HOWTO defines it as a means of tracking events that happen when some software runs: the developer adds logging calls to the code to indicate that certain events have occurred, and each event is described by a message and has an importance, which is called its level or severity (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter introduces the logging module as a way to create a record of custom messages that describes when execution reached a call and which values the variables held (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Logging is the practice of making a program write down what it does while it runs. The Python logging HOWTO defines it as a means of tracking events that happen when some software runs: the developer adds logging calls to the code to indicate that certain events have occurred, and each event is described by a message and has an importance, which is called its level or severity (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter introduces the logging module as a way to create a record of custom messages that describes when execution reached a call and which values the variables held (Sweigart, 2025).

Logging gives the programmer a trail of breadcrumbs that can help to work out when things started to go wrong, and a missing message tells equally clearly that a part of the code was skipped (Sweigart, 2025). Unlike a bare print call, a log message has a level, a time and a destination, and all of them can be changed without editing the lines that produce the messages. That makes it possible to leave the calls in a finished program and still silence them.

Logging is met in the chapter's factorial program, in the terminal output of nearly every large Python tool and in the log files of servers. The logging module is part of the standard library, so a program needs only to import it. The same module serves a three-line script and a large application, by the same four ideas: a logger that receives the calls, a handler that decides where a message goes, a level that decides which messages count, and a format that decides how a message looks.

This branch has four parts. Setup explains the call that configures the system, the format, the destination and the rule by which a second configuration is ignored. Loggers and handlers explains the objects behind the simple calls. Levels explains the five levels, the threshold, the default and the way of switching everything off. Practice explains why logging is better than print and how to write the calls well.

nodes.label: Setup
nodes.body: Setting up logging means telling the module three things: which messages count, how a message should look and where it should go. The chapter does all three with one call placed at the top of the program, logging.basicConfig, with the arguments level, format and, optionally, filename (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Setting up logging means telling the module three things: which messages count, how a message should look and where it should go. The chapter does all three with one call placed at the top of the program, logging.basicConfig, with the arguments level, format and, optionally, filename (Sweigart, 2025).

Without a setup a program prints only warnings and worse, in a fixed shape, to the error stream. The setup is what turns logging into a debugging tool for the programmer: lowering the threshold to DEBUG shows everything, and a format with a time shows the order and the pace of events.

The concepts of this group follow the order of the arguments. basicConfig itself comes first, then the format string and the percent placeholders it is written with, then the log file, and then the rule that makes a second call of basicConfig do nothing unless it is forced.

The three arguments can be watched working together in one call. A level of DEBUG lowers the threshold so that every message is shown, the format decides the text around each message, and a filename sends them to a file instead of the error stream (Sweigart, 2025). The call takes effect once only: a second logging.basicConfig does nothing, so a program that configures DEBUG and then configures ERROR still shows its debug messages, unless force=True is passed, which removes the existing handlers first (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Basic config
nodes.body: The function logging.basicConfig does the basic configuration of the logging system. According to the library reference it creates a StreamHandler with a default Formatter and adds it to the root logger, and its keyword arguments choose the level, the format string, a file name, a stream and a few other options (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter lets the reader copy two lines to the top of a program: import logging, and logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s') (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The function logging.basicConfig does the basic configuration of the logging system. According to the library reference it creates a StreamHandler with a default Formatter and adds it to the root logger, and its keyword arguments choose the level, the format string, a file name, a stream and a few other options (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter lets the reader copy two lines to the top of a program: import logging, and logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s') (Sweigart, 2025).

The call is the shortest path from no logging to useful logging. It makes the standard messages visible and gives them a layout, and the programmer does not have to learn about loggers and handlers first. The HOWTO says that for simple usage a format with the level name, the message and perhaps the time of the event is all that is needed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The call is placed once, near the top of the main program, before any message is logged. The HOWTO states that the call should come before any calls to a logger's methods such as debug() and info(), otherwise that logging event may not be handled in the desired manner (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the chapter it stands under the import of the logging module in factorialLog.py.

A program that calls logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format='%(levelname)s - %(message)s') and then logs a debug message and an info message prints DEBUG - Start of program and INFO - going on, on the error stream. The functions debug, info, warning, error and critical call basicConfig automatically if no handlers are defined for the root logger (Python Software Foundation, 2026), which is why the chapter's description of debug() as calling basicConfig is true only when the program has not configured logging itself.

The call can be silently ignored. It does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, which includes the case where an earlier logging call has configured the system implicitly, and a later concept shows the effect. Also, basicConfig must be called from the main thread before other threads are started (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Keep it at the very top of the program.

nodes.definition: basicConfig sets the threshold, the format and the destination of the root logger; the chapter calls it once at the top of a program.

nodes.label: Log format
nodes.body: The log format is a string that describes the layout of each line a log call produces. It is a template in which named fields, written in the form %(name)s, stand for the parts of a log record. The chapter's template, %(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s, puts the time, the level name and the message, separated by dashes, on every line (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The log format is a string that describes the layout of each line a log call produces. It is a template in which named fields, written in the form %(name)s, stand for the parts of a log record. The chapter's template, %(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s, puts the time, the level name and the message, separated by dashes, on every line (Sweigart, 2025).

The format decides how useful a log is when read later. The time shows how long a step took, the level shows how serious the line is, and the message says what happened. A format that adds the function name or the line number lets the reader find the call that produced a line.

The format string is passed to basicConfig as the format argument. The library reference lists the fields of a log record that can be used: asctime is the human-readable time at which the record was created, of the form 2003-07-08 16:49:45,896 where the digits after the comma are milliseconds; levelname is the text of the level; message is the logged message; and others such as funcName and lineno name the place of the call (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

When no format is given, basicConfig uses the default, which has the attributes levelname, name and message separated by colons (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so logging.warning('Watch out!') prints WARNING:root:Watch out!. With the format '%(levelname)s - %(message)s' the same record is shown as WARNING - Watch out!. The chapter's printed times, such as 2035-05-23 16:20:12,664, are illustrations; a real run prints the clock time of the machine, in the same shape.

A field name that is not an attribute of the record does not stop the program. The logging package is designed to swallow exceptions that occur while logging, so for the format '%(nofield)s' the first message produces a --- Logging error --- report with a traceback on the error stream, ending in ValueError: Formatting field not found in record: 'nofield', and the program carries on (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Write the field list carefully, with the letter s that follows each closing parenthesis. The style argument of basicConfig lets a format use braces or dollar signs instead of percent signs, but the percent style is the default and the one the chapter uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: A format string with named fields decides what each log line shows; the chapter's shows time, level and message.

nodes.label: Percent placeholder
nodes.body: A percent placeholder is a marker such as %s or %d in a string that is replaced by a value. The Python reference calls the % operator on strings the string formatting or interpolation operator: given format % values, the conversion specifications in the format are replaced with elements of values, as in the example '%s has %d quote types.' % ('Python', 2), which gives 'Python has 2 quote types.' (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A conversion specification starts with the % character; s converts any object with str and d stands for a signed decimal integer.

paras.text: A percent placeholder is a marker such as %s or %d in a string that is replaced by a value. The Python reference calls the % operator on strings the string formatting or interpolation operator: given format % values, the conversion specifications in the format are replaced with elements of values, as in the example '%s has %d quote types.' % ('Python', 2), which gives 'Python has 2 quote types.' (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A conversion specification starts with the % character; s converts any object with str and d stands for a signed decimal integer.

The logging module is older than formatted string literals, and the logging HOWTO explains that merging variable data into a message uses this old, percent style for backwards compatibility (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A learner who meets logging.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total) in real code needs to read the markers, and the log format string of basicConfig is written in the same notation.

The markers appear in two places in logging: in the message of a log call, where each marker is filled from the arguments that follow the message, and in the format string, where a marker with a name in parentheses, such as %(levelname)s, is filled from the attributes of the log record. The second form is the one that takes its values from a dictionary, which maps names to values; the reference shows '%(language)s has %(number)03d quote types.' filled with a dictionary, giving 'Python has 002 quote types.' (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Python scans the string for markers and fills them in order from a tuple, or by name from a dictionary. The count must fit: '%s %s' % ('a',) raises a TypeError with the message not enough arguments for format string, and '%s' % (1, 2) raises one with not all arguments converted during string formatting. The logging module avoids both at the call: it merges the message and the arguments only when a record is emitted, and a message given no arguments is not formatted at all (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A literal percent sign in a message that has arguments must be written as %%, because a lone one starts a conversion. The reference itself notes that the operations have quirks that lead to common errors, and recommends formatted string literals, str.format() or string.Template as alternatives for ordinary text (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In ordinary code use an f-string; in the arguments of a log call use the markers.

nodes.definition: The old-style way of putting values into a string: % conversion specifications in the string are replaced by the values to the right of the % operator.

nodes.label: Log to file
nodes.body: Logging to a file means sending the log messages to a text file instead of the screen. A file is a named sequence of characters kept on disk, and a text file can be read in any text editor. The chapter passes a filename named argument to basicConfig, as in logging.basicConfig(filename='myProgramLog.txt', level=logging.DEBUG, format=...), and the log messages are saved to myProgramLog.txt (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Logging to a file means sending the log messages to a text file instead of the screen. A file is a named sequence of characters kept on disk, and a text file can be read in any text editor. The chapter passes a filename named argument to basicConfig, as in logging.basicConfig(filename='myProgramLog.txt', level=logging.DEBUG, format=...), and the log messages are saved to myProgramLog.txt (Sweigart, 2025).

Messages on the screen clutter the output of the program and disappear when the window is closed. Written to a file, they keep the screen clear and can be read after the program has run, as the chapter points out (Sweigart, 2025). A file is also the only practical place for the log of a program that runs without anyone watching it.

The option is used when a program runs unattended or writes more messages than anyone would read on a screen, and the file is read afterwards with an editor or a program. The library reference explains the mechanism: specifying filename makes basicConfig create a FileHandler with that name, rather than a StreamHandler (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The file is opened in the mode given by filemode, which defaults to 'a' (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and the HOWTO explains the result: if the script is run several times, the messages of successive runs are appended to the file, and a filemode of 'w' makes every run start afresh (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In a test in which a short program is run twice with the same file name, the file holds two lines DEBUG - run; run twice again with filemode='w', it holds one.

By default the file grows indefinitely, as the FileHandler documentation warns (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so a long-lived program needs a plan for old logs. The HOWTO's file example also passes encoding='utf-8', so that text such as Malmö is written correctly; the glossary explains that a string has to be serialized as a sequence of bytes to be stored, and the text encoding is the rule for that (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And an argument conflict is an error: the library reference says that stream is incompatible with filename, and that giving both raises a ValueError (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: Passing filename to basicConfig sends the messages to a text file instead of the screen.

nodes.label: Force reconfigure
nodes.body: Force reconfigure is the option that makes basicConfig replace an existing configuration. The library reference states that the function does nothing if the root logger already has handlers configured, unless the keyword argument force is set to true, in which case the existing handlers are removed and closed before the new configuration is carried out (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The argument was added in Python 3.8.

paras.text: Force reconfigure is the option that makes basicConfig replace an existing configuration. The library reference states that the function does nothing if the root logger already has handlers configured, unless the keyword argument force is set to true, in which case the existing handlers are removed and closed before the new configuration is carried out (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The argument was added in Python 3.8.

The rule is a frequent source of confusion, because the second call fails silently. A learner who changes the level in a program, or experiments in an interactive session, sees no effect and no error. Knowing the rule, and the one-word remedy, saves a lot of puzzling.

It is met in the interactive shell, where earlier lines have already configured logging, in test suites, and in programs in which a library configures logging before the main program does. The chapter does not mention the rule.

A program that calls basicConfig with level WARNING and the format 'first %(message)s', then again with level DEBUG and the format 'second %(message)s', and then logs a debug and a warning message prints only first w, because the second call is ignored. After a third call with force=True and the format 'third %(message)s', a debug message prints third d2.

An implicit configuration counts too. The call logging.warning('first') configures the root logger by itself, because it has no handlers, and a later basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is then ignored: a following logging.debug call prints nothing and the level of the root logger is still 30. Place basicConfig before any other logging call, or use force=True when the order cannot be controlled.

nodes.definition: basicConfig does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, so a second call is ignored unless force=True is passed.

nodes.label: Loggers and handlers
nodes.body: Behind the simple module-level functions of logging stands a small system of objects. The Python documentation says that the library takes a modular approach and offers several categories of components: loggers expose the interface that application code uses, handlers send the log records to the right destination, filters decide finer which records to output, and formatters specify the layout of the final output (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Behind the simple module-level functions of logging stands a small system of objects. The Python documentation says that the library takes a modular approach and offers several categories of components: loggers expose the interface that application code uses, handlers send the log records to the right destination, filters decide finer which records to output, and formatters specify the layout of the final output (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The system explains behaviour that the one-line setup hides: why a message from one part of a program can be shown while another is not, why a message can appear twice, and why basicConfig can be ignored. A learner who knows the logger, the handler and the record can read the documentation of logging and the logs of larger programs.

The concepts of this group are the logger, which receives the calls and chooses by level, the handler, which delivers the record to a destination, and the log record, the object that carries the details of one event from the first to the second. Log information is passed between loggers, handlers, filters and formatters in a LogRecord instance (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The objects explain the two puzzles the one-line setup leaves behind. A message has to pass two thresholds, the logger's and the handler's, so a logger set to DEBUG whose handler is set to WARNING shows the warning and swallows the debug message, which is why lowering one threshold alone can look like doing nothing (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A message also travels from a logger to its ancestors, so a logger that has a handler of its own and still passes messages up to the root logger produces the same line twice, and that is the usual cause of a doubled log.

nodes.label: Logger
nodes.body: A logger is the object on which log calls are made. Each logger has a name, and the names are arranged in a hierarchy by dots, so that the logger 'app.db' is a child of 'app', and all loggers are descendants of the root logger. A logger is always obtained from logging.getLogger(name), and calls with the same name return the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A logger is the object on which log calls are made. Each logger has a name, and the names are arranged in a hierarchy by dots, so that the logger 'app.db' is a child of 'app', and all loggers are descendants of the root logger. A logger is always obtained from logging.getLogger(name), and calls with the same name return the same object (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Loggers let the parts of a large program log separately. A name such as the one a module has, which the documentation recommends for the purpose, tells the reader where a message came from, and the threshold of one logger can be changed without touching the others. A library written by someone else can log through its own logger and leave the choices to the application (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the chapter a logger is present but not named: the functions logging.debug, logging.info, logging.warning, logging.error and logging.critical just call the same-named method of the root logger, whose name is printed as root in the output (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Larger programs write logger = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top of each module, where __name__ is the module's name.

In a check, the call logging.getLogger() returns an object of the class RootLogger whose name is 'root', logging.getLogger('app') is logging.getLogger('app') is True, and once the logger 'app' exists the parent of logging.getLogger('app.db') is the logger named 'app'. A new logger has no level of its own, so its effective level is that of its nearest ancestor with one; for 'app.db' that is the root's level, 30, unless something sets another (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The documentation says that loggers should never be created directly but always through the function getLogger (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A message from a named logger is also handled differently when nothing is configured: it is printed as the bare message by the handler of last resort, instead of in the root format. Do not log to the root logger in a library, so that the application can configure it as it likes (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: The object that receives log calls; the module-level functions use the root logger, and named loggers form a hierarchy by dotted names.

nodes.label: Handler
nodes.body: A handler is the object that delivers a log record to a destination. The logging documentation lists several: a StreamHandler writes to a stream and uses sys.stderr when none is given, a FileHandler writes to a disk file, and there are handlers for email and for system logs, among others (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler also has its own level, which starts as NOTSET so that every record is processed.

paras.text: A handler is the object that delivers a log record to a destination. The logging documentation lists several: a StreamHandler writes to a stream and uses sys.stderr when none is given, a FileHandler writes to a disk file, and there are handlers for email and for system logs, among others (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A handler also has its own level, which starts as NOTSET so that every record is processed.

Handlers separate what is logged from where it goes. The same record can be sent to the screen and to a file, each with its own format and threshold, without changing the line that logs it. This separation is what makes it possible to change the destination of a whole program by changing its setup only.

In the chapter handlers are created for the reader by basicConfig. Without a filename it makes a StreamHandler, and with filename it makes a FileHandler (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The list of the handlers of the root logger is available as logging.getLogger().handlers: it is the empty list in a program that has not logged anything, and after logging.basicConfig() it holds one handler of the class StreamHandler.

When a logger accepts a call, it creates a record and offers it to its handlers, and then, if its propagate attribute is true, to the handlers of its parent loggers. If no handler is found in the whole chain, the handler of last resort is used, a StreamHandler writing to sys.stderr with the level WARNING (Python Software Foundation, 2026). That explains why a warning from an unconfigured named logger still appears on the screen while its info messages do not.

Do not attach the same handler to a logger and to its ancestors: the documentation warns that a record may then be emitted several times (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The reason why basicConfig does nothing on a second call is that it checks whether the root logger already has handlers.

nodes.definition: The object that sends a log record to a destination; basicConfig creates a StreamHandler for the screen or, with filename, a FileHandler for a file.

nodes.label: Log record
nodes.body: A log record is the object that a logger creates for each event that is logged. It contains all the information pertinent to the event: the name of the logger, the numeric level, the path and line number of the call, the message and the arguments to merge into it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Records are created automatically; the logging reference notes that they can also be made by hand.

paras.text: A log record is the object that a logger creates for each event that is logged. It contains all the information pertinent to the event: the name of the logger, the numeric level, the path and line number of the call, the message and the arguments to merge into it (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Records are created automatically; the logging reference notes that they can also be made by hand.

The record is the common currency of the logging system. Loggers, handlers, filters and formatters all work on records, and the fields of the record are the names that a format string can use. Knowing what a record holds shows what a log line can contain.

A record is never seen in the simple use of the chapter, but its attributes are what the format string selects: asctime, levelname and message are all attributes of the record (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The attribute levelname is the text of the level, 'INFO' for 20, and levelno is the number.

The message of a record is computed as msg % args when it is needed. With msg equal to 'hello %s' and args equal to ('world',), the call getMessage() returns 'hello world', and the record created for a level of 20 has the levelname 'INFO'. If a message is given without arguments, no percent formatting is done, so the message '100%' is returned as it is (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The record is created only if the logger is enabled for the level of the call, so a call below the threshold is cheap: in a test that counts how many records are created, a debug call to a logger whose threshold is WARNING creates none and a warning call creates one. The formatted message and the time are computed later, when the record is handled. Arbitrary objects can also be used as the message, in which case str is called on them to produce the text (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: The object created for every logging event; it carries the logger name, the level, the message and its arguments, and the place of the call.

nodes.label: Levels
nodes.body: Levels are the importance ranks that log messages carry. There are five of them, from the least to the most important, and each has a name, a number and a function of the same name. The chapter describes them in Table 5-1 and explains that logging levels provide a way to categorise log messages by importance, so that less important messages can be filtered out while testing (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Levels are the importance ranks that log messages carry. There are five of them, from the least to the most important, and each has a name, a number and a function of the same name. The chapter describes them in Table 5-1 and explains that logging levels provide a way to categorise log messages by importance, so that less important messages can be filtered out while testing (Sweigart, 2025).

The levels allow one program to produce a lot of output while it is being developed and little when it is finished, without changing any logging call. The programmer decides the level of each message once, and the setup decides which levels are shown. This turns logging into a dial that can be turned from detailed to silent.

The group has four concepts: the five levels and their numbers, the threshold that selects among them, the default threshold that applies when nothing has been configured, and logging.disable, which silences levels from outside the program's own setup.

The ranks are numbers, and that is what makes a threshold a comparison. DEBUG is 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30, ERROR 40 and CRITICAL 50, and a message is shown when its number is at least the threshold's, so a threshold of WARNING hides DEBUG and INFO and shows the other three (Sweigart, 2025). With no setup at all the root logger's threshold is WARNING, which is why a program whose only logging call is logging.debug appears to do nothing, and logging.disable silences every level up to the one it is given, from outside the program's own setup.

nodes.label: Logging levels
nodes.body: The five logging levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL, in increasing order of importance. Each is a number in the logging module: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, and a sixth value, NOTSET, which is 0, means that no level is set (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter gives the five names with the functions that log at each level: logging.debug(), logging.info(), logging.warning(), logging.error() and logging.critical() (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The five logging levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR and CRITICAL, in increasing order of importance. Each is a number in the logging module: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50, and a sixth value, NOTSET, which is 0, means that no level is set (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter gives the five names with the functions that log at each level: logging.debug(), logging.info(), logging.warning(), logging.error() and logging.critical() (Sweigart, 2025).

A level states how much attention a message deserves. The chapter explains them in its Table 5-1: DEBUG is the lowest level, used for small details that matter only when diagnosing problems; INFO records general events or confirms that the program works; WARNING indicates a potential problem that does not yet stop the program; ERROR records an error that made the program fail to do something; and CRITICAL is the highest level, for a fatal error that has caused, or is about to cause, the program to stop (Sweigart, 2025).

Each level is used by calling the function with the same name as the level in lower case. A program that sets the level to DEBUG with format '%(levelname)s - %(message)s' and logs one message at each level prints DEBUG - d, INFO - i, WARNING - w, ERROR - e and CRITICAL - c, in the order of the calls.

The numbers make the comparison of importance possible: a message is accepted if its number is not lower than the threshold. The module defines the five names as constants, so logging.DEBUG is the number 10 and logging.CRITICAL is 50. Levels of one's own can be defined with logging.addLevelName, but all levels used must be registered with it, and the documentation calls a custom level higher than CRITICAL not recommended (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The level of a message is the programmer's judgment, not a property that Python can check: as the chapter says, it is up to you to decide which category your log message falls into (Sweigart, 2025). Do not use CRITICAL for routine trouble, since a level that is used for everything no longer separates anything.

nodes.definition: The five levels run from lowest to highest importance, and each has a number: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50.

nodes.label: Level threshold
nodes.body: The level threshold is the level below which messages are ignored. It is set with the level argument of basicConfig, and a logger set to a threshold accepts messages of that level and above. The documentation of setLevel says that messages less severe than the level will be ignored, and messages of that severity or higher are emitted, unless a handler's own level is higher (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The level threshold is the level below which messages are ignored. It is set with the level argument of basicConfig, and a logger set to a threshold accepts messages of that level and above. The documentation of setLevel says that messages less severe than the level will be ignored, and messages of that severity or higher are emitted, unless a handler's own level is higher (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The threshold is the dial of the chapter's logging system. During development it is DEBUG, which the chapter says shows messages from all the logging levels. Later, when the programmer is interested only in errors, level=logging.ERROR shows only ERROR and CRITICAL messages and skips the DEBUG, INFO and WARNING messages (Sweigart, 2025).

It is set once, in the setup of the program, and often read from a setting so that a user can ask for more detail without editing the program. The HOWTO shows how to turn a command-line option such as --log=INFO into the number to pass as level, with getattr(logging, loglevel.upper()) (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In a program that sets level=logging.ERROR and logs one message at each level, only ERROR - e and CRITICAL - c appear. The comparison uses the numbers: 40 and 50 are not lower than the threshold 40, whereas 10, 20 and 30 are. Nothing is deleted or changed in the logging calls; changing the one word in the setup brings the other messages back.

There are two thresholds, one in the logger and one in each handler, and a message must pass both. The logger's level is checked first; a handler with a higher level of its own will drop the record afterwards. If a message does not appear although the logger's level is low enough, look at the level of the handler.

nodes.definition: A message is shown only if its level is at least the threshold, so raising the threshold hides the lower levels without deleting any call.

nodes.label: Default level
nodes.body: The default level is the threshold that applies when the program has not configured logging. The documentation states that the default level is WARNING, which means that only events of this severity and higher are tracked unless the logging package is configured to do otherwise, and that the root logger is created with the level WARNING (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The default level is the threshold that applies when the program has not configured logging. The documentation states that the default level is WARNING, which means that only events of this severity and higher are tracked unless the logging package is configured to do otherwise, and that the root logger is created with the level WARNING (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The default explains a very common surprise. A learner writes logging.debug('value is 3') and sees nothing, because debug messages are below the default threshold. The chapter avoids the surprise by always calling basicConfig with level=logging.DEBUG first (Sweigart, 2025).

The default is met in any program that imports logging and logs without a setup, in the interactive shell, and in code that libraries run. In such a program logging.warning('Watch out!') prints WARNING:root:Watch out!, and logging.info('I told you so') prints nothing, as the HOWTO shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The expression logging.getLogger().getEffectiveLevel() evaluates to 30 in a fresh program, the number of WARNING. The functions logging.warning and logging.error find no handler on the root logger, and so they call basicConfig themselves, with the default format, to the error stream; a program that calls logging.warning('w') and logging.error('e') prints WARNING:root:w and ERROR:root:e. A named logger that has no configuration at all is served by the handler of last resort, which prints the bare message, such as bare, for WARNING and above (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The side effect on the root logger is the trap: after the first implicit call the root logger has a handler, so a later basicConfig is ignored. Debug messages that are missing from the output are therefore explained by the default threshold or by an earlier implicit configuration, and the fix is level=logging.DEBUG in a first call of basicConfig or force=True.

nodes.definition: Without basicConfig the threshold is WARNING, so debug and info calls print nothing and warning and error calls print to standard error.

nodes.label: Disabling logging
nodes.body: Disabling logging means switching log messages off from one place, without deleting the calls. The function logging.disable(level) provides an overriding level for all loggers, which takes precedence over each logger's own level, and its effect is to disable all logging calls of severity level and below (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's recipe is logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL), which suppresses all log messages (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Disabling logging means switching log messages off from one place, without deleting the calls. The function logging.disable(level) provides an overriding level for all loggers, which takes precedence over each logger's own level, and its effect is to disable all logging calls of severity level and below (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's recipe is logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL), which suppresses all log messages (Sweigart, 2025).

A finished program should not fill the screen with debugging messages, and deleting the calls would make the next debugging session start from nothing. A single line that can be commented out or in turns all the messages on and off. The chapter advises putting it near the import logging line so that it is easy to find (Sweigart, 2025).

It is used at the end of development, in tests that should run quietly, and in a program that wants a global quiet switch. Called with no argument, it uses the level CRITICAL, which is the default since Python 3.7 (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In a program that sets level=logging.INFO, logs a critical message, calls logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) and logs again, the first message appears as CRITICAL - before and the later critical and error messages are silent. Calling logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) removes the override, so a following error message appears as ERROR - after. A call with logging.INFO discards INFO and DEBUG events only, so a later warning still prints.

The disable level applies to all loggers in the process, including those of libraries, and it overrides their own settings, so a program that disables logging for a test must undo it. The setting is a number: logging.disable(logging.NOTSET) is the way back, not logging.enable, which does not exist.

nodes.definition: logging.disable silences the given level and all below it; disabling CRITICAL turns every message off, and NOTSET turns them back on.

nodes.label: Practice
nodes.body: Practice in logging is the set of habits that decide whether log messages help or hinder. The first habit is to choose logging and not print for the diagnostic output of a program, and the second is to write the log calls so that they cost little when the messages are not wanted.

paras.text: Practice in logging is the set of habits that decide whether log messages help or hinder. The first habit is to choose logging and not print for the diagnostic output of a program, and the second is to write the log calls so that they cost little when the messages are not wanted.

A log that is easy to switch off, and cheap when off, is a log the programmer will leave in the program. A log full of expensive string building is one that has to be removed before the program is released, which brings back the problem that logging was meant to solve.

The two concepts are the comparison of logging with print, which the chapter makes in its section A Poor Practice and in its practice questions, and the lazy formatting of messages, which the logging documentation explains.

Both habits are justified by what the module does rather than by taste. A logging call is switched off by one line of setup while a print has to be found and deleted, and the log line carries a level and a time that a print does not (Sweigart, 2025). Lazy formatting is the second habit: passing the values after the message, as logging.debug with a placeholder and its value does, leaves the formatting to the module, which performs it only when the message is actually going to be shown, whereas building the string first performs it on every call even when the result is thrown away (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.label: Logging versus print
nodes.body: Logging and print both write text, but they serve different readers. The chapter's rule is that log messages are intended for the programmer, not the user, and that for error messages the user should see, like File not found or Invalid input, please enter a number, a print call is the right tool (Sweigart, 2025). The practice question that asks why logging messages are better than print calls for the same message has the answer in the same section.

paras.text: Logging and print both write text, but they serve different readers. The chapter's rule is that log messages are intended for the programmer, not the user, and that for error messages the user should see, like File not found or Invalid input, please enter a number, a print call is the right tool (Sweigart, 2025). The practice question that asks why logging messages are better than print calls for the same message has the answer in the same section.

The chapter calls debugging with print a poor practice. When the debugging is done, the programmer has to remove each print call, and may accidentally remove calls that were used for non-log messages. With logging, a program may be filled with as many messages as the programmer likes and all of them can be disabled later with one logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) call (Sweigart, 2025).

The Python logging HOWTO sets the same division in a table: to display console output for the ordinary usage of a command line script or program, use print; to report events that occur during normal operation, such as for status monitoring or fault investigation, use a logger's info or debug method (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Each log call also adds a level and, if the format asks for it, a time, and it goes by default to the error stream, whereas print goes to the standard output. A program that prints one line with print and logs one line with logging.warning shows both until logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL) is called; after it only the print line remains.

The distinction is easy to blur in small scripts: a message the user needs, such as the result of the calculation, must be printed, and must not depend on the logging setup, or it would vanish when logging is disabled. The chapter's factorial program makes the point: print(factorial(5)) is part of the original program, so the code displays the result even if logging messages are disabled (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.definition: Log messages are for the programmer and print is for the user; log calls stay in the program and one setting switches them all off, where print calls would each have to be deleted.

nodes.label: Lazy formatting
nodes.body: Lazy formatting means that the text of a log message is built only if the message is actually going to be emitted. A call such as log.debug('value is %s', obj) hands the message and the argument separately to the logger; the HOWTO says that formatting of message arguments is deferred until it cannot be avoided (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An f-string, by contrast, builds the whole text before the call is made.

paras.text: Lazy formatting means that the text of a log message is built only if the message is actually going to be emitted. A call such as log.debug('value is %s', obj) hands the message and the argument separately to the logger; the HOWTO says that formatting of message arguments is deferred until it cannot be avoided (Python Software Foundation, 2026). An f-string, by contrast, builds the whole text before the call is made.

Building a message can be costly, for example when an object has a long text form, and a program that logs inside a loop may build thousands of messages that no one will read. With deferred formatting a disabled debug call costs little more than the call itself, which makes it affordable to leave such calls in a finished program.

The form is common in the code of libraries and of larger applications, which pass the values after the message as in log.debug('i is %s, total is %s', i, total). The percent markers are the ones explained under percent placeholders.

A small experiment shows the difference. A class is a recipe for objects, and the method __str__ is what Python calls to turn an object into text; here it counts its calls. With the level at INFO, log.debug('value is %s', obj) leaves the count at 0, log.debug(f'value is {obj}') raises it to 1 although nothing is printed, and log.info('value is %s', obj) raises it to 2 and prints INFO:demo:value is noisy.

Lazy formatting defers only the formatting. The arguments themselves are evaluated before the call, so an expensive function call among them still runs. The HOWTO's advice is to guard such a call with if logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG), so that the expensive functions are never called when the logger's threshold is above DEBUG (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

nodes.definition: A message given arguments is formatted only when it is emitted, so a disabled debug call costs no string conversion, unlike an f-string built before the call.

nodes.label: Debugger
nodes.body: The debugger is a tool that runs a program one instruction at a time and lets the programmer look at the program between the steps. The chapter defines it as a feature of the Mu editor that executes a program one instruction at a time, giving a chance to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). A program started this way is said to run under the debugger. The same idea is offered by IDLE, by other editor software, and by the module pdb, the Python debugger, which ships with Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The debugger is a tool that runs a program one instruction at a time and lets the programmer look at the program between the steps. The chapter defines it as a feature of the Mu editor that executes a program one instruction at a time, giving a chance to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). A program started this way is said to run under the debugger. The same idea is offered by IDLE, by other editor software, and by the module pdb, the Python debugger, which ships with Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The debugger shows what a program actually does instead of what its author thinks it does. The chapter admits that the process is much slower than running the program at full speed, but it lets the programmer see the actual values in a program while it runs, rather than deduce what the values might be from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Exceptions, assertions and logging must be written into the program before it runs, and a question that the programmer did not think of in advance cannot be answered by them. The debugger can be started without changing the program, and then any variable can be read at any point.

The chapter teaches the debugger inside the Mu editor, with buttons and a pane at the side of the window. The same tool is found in IDLE, whose documentation lists a debugger with persistent breakpoints and stepping among its features, and in the module pdb, which is part of the standard library and is controlled by typing short commands at a prompt (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The built-in function breakpoint() lets a program start the debugger by itself at a chosen line, and since Python 3.14 pdb can also attach to a program that is already running.

The branch has three groups. The first, the debugger interface, describes what the person sees: the editor, the act of running under the debugger, the pane that lists the variables, and the button that stops the session. The second, the controls, describes how the person moves through the program: breakpoints, Continue, Step In, Step Over and Step Out. The third, the Python debugger, shows the same controls as commands of pdb and explains breakpoint(), the environment variable that configures it, and attaching to a running process.

The debugger shows only the values that the program has at the moment it is paused. It does not remember how the values got there, so a bug whose cause lies far back in the run can still require several sessions or a log. The chapter also reminds the reader that a program that waits for typed input still waits under the debugger (Sweigart, 2025). Finally, the debugger is a convenience of the editor or of pdb and not a feature of the language, so the buttons and wording of one tool do not carry over unchanged to another.

nodes.label: Debugger interface
nodes.body: The debugger interface is everything the person at the keyboard sees and touches while a program runs under the debugger. The chapter describes it for the Mu editor: the editor window in which the debugger is started, the Debug button that starts it, the Debug Inspector pane that lists the values of the variables, and the Stop button that ends the session (Sweigart, 2025). These four parts are the subject of the concepts in this group.

paras.text: The debugger interface is everything the person at the keyboard sees and touches while a program runs under the debugger. The chapter describes it for the Mu editor: the editor window in which the debugger is started, the Debug button that starts it, the Debug Inspector pane that lists the values of the variables, and the Stop button that ends the session (Sweigart, 2025). These four parts are the subject of the concepts in this group.

The same four parts exist in every debugger, even though their look differs. IDLE starts its debugger from a toggle in a menu and marks breakpoints through a context menu (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and pdb replaces buttons and panes with commands typed at a prompt and answers printed as text. A student who knows what each part is for can therefore use whichever tool is at hand, and can read a transcript of a debugging session without having the window in front of them.

The concepts follow the order of a debugging session: the editor in which it takes place, running a program under the debugger so that it pauses before its first line, reading the program state in the inspector pane, and stopping the program. The controls that move the program forward, namely breakpoints, Continue and the three kinds of step, belong to the next group. Because the windows of Mu cannot be reproduced in text, the transcripts quoted in this group were produced by running pdb on the same kind of program.

Because the editor's windows cannot be reproduced in text, the same session is shown here in pdb, where every part has a name that can be typed. Starting a file with python -m pdb halts the program before its first line and prints that line at a prompt, the commands p and args read the program's state in place of the inspector pane, c continues the program and q ends the session as the Stop button does (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The parts map one to one onto the editor's buttons, which is what lets a transcript stand in for a screenshot without anything being lost.

nodes.label: Mu editor
nodes.body: Mu is the code editor that the chapter uses for its programs. An editor is a program for writing source code, and Mu adds to it the means to run a program and to run it under the debugger. The chapter says that the debugger is a feature of the Mu editor, IDLE, and other editor software (Sweigart, 2025). In Mu the top row of buttons has a Run button and, next to it, a Debug button, and the file being edited is shown in a file editor with a number for each line.

paras.text: Mu is the code editor that the chapter uses for its programs. An editor is a program for writing source code, and Mu adds to it the means to run a program and to run it under the debugger. The chapter says that the debugger is a feature of the Mu editor, IDLE, and other editor software (Sweigart, 2025). In Mu the top row of buttons has a Run button and, next to it, a Debug button, and the file being edited is shown in a file editor with a number for each line.

A named editor gives the instructions of the chapter something to refer to. The chapter's instructions say to click a button or to click a line number, and they are only understandable if the reader knows which window and which button are meant. The editor is also where the program's text, its output and its debugger meet: the program is edited in the file editor, a running program writes into the output pane, and, as the chapter notes, a program that calls input() waits for the answer to be typed into that output pane (Sweigart, 2025).

The window of Mu appears in the figures of the chapter. Figure 5-1 shows the program paused before its first line, with that line highlighted in the file editor, and Figure 5-3 shows the pane at the right with the variables of the adding program (Sweigart, 2025). Other editors offer the same facilities under other names. The IDLE page of the Python documentation, for example, describes a Debugger entry that makes code entered in the Shell or run from an Editor run under the debugger, and IDLE is described in the glossary as an editor and interpreter environment that ships with the standard distribution of Python (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Starting the debugger in Mu is a matter of clicking Debug instead of Run. The Debug Inspector pane then opens at the right side of the window, and Debugging mode adds the buttons Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out to the top of the editor, next to the usual Stop button (Sweigart, 2025). Everything else, editing the text and saving the file, works as before. The same program can therefore be run in the two ways one after the other, which is how the chapter proceeds with its adding program.

Mu is one editor among many, and its buttons and menus are not part of Python. The chapter itself remarks that Mu should prevent the debugger from entering Python's built-in functions (Sweigart, 2025), a convenience that a command-line debugger does not necessarily share. The IDLE documentation warns that its debugger is still incomplete and somewhat experimental (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When a button named in the chapter is not found in another editor, the underlying idea, pause, look, step, continue, is what to search for.

nodes.example: the Mu window with a Debug button next to Run
nodes.definition: The code editor used in the chapter; it has a Run button, a Debug button and a Debug Inspector pane, and its output pane is where a running program receives typed input.

nodes.label: Running under the debugger
nodes.body: Running a program under the debugger means starting it through the debugger instead of running it directly. The program does not run to its end at once. It is paused just before its first line of code and waits for the programmer to say what to do next. In Mu the Debug button, next to the Run button, starts this mode, and the first line, the one about to be executed, is highlighted in the file editor (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Running a program under the debugger means starting it through the debugger instead of running it directly. The program does not run to its end at once. It is paused just before its first line of code and waits for the programmer to say what to do next. In Mu the Debug button, next to the Run button, starts this mode, and the first line, the one about to be executed, is highlighted in the file editor (Sweigart, 2025).

A normal run gives no chance to look inside: the program starts, prints its output and ends, and the programmer sees only the result. Under the debugger the programmer gets control before the first line and after every step, which is the only way to watch a variable change from line to line. The price, in the chapter's words, is speed: the process is much slower than running the program at full speed (Sweigart, 2025). The mode is therefore used on a program that is already known to misbehave, such as the adding program that prints 5342.

The command-line debugger is started with the command python -m pdb followed by the name of the file. The documentation says that, as with a script, the debugger pauses execution just before the first line of a module started this way (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript the program starts with a line def double(x): and the first thing the debugger prints is > main.py(1)<module>() followed by -> def double(x):. The first line names the file and the line number in parentheses, with <module> standing for the top level of the file, outside any function, and the second line shows the instruction that is about to run.

The debugger then prints its prompt, (Pdb), and waits for a command. After the command n, which executes the current line and pauses at the next one in the same function, the next stop is on line 4, val = 3, because lines 2 and 3 belong to the function that line 1 only defines; after another n the stop is on line 5, result = double(val). Lines 2 and 3 run only when the function is called. This shows that the debugger moves through the lines in the order in which they execute, not the order in which they are written.

Running under the debugger changes nothing about what the program does, only when it does it, so effects such as printing, asking for input, or writing a file all still happen. If the program ends, pdb reports that the program finished and will be restarted and stops again before the first line, as the executed run of the coin program shows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And ending the session with the quit command aborts the program being executed, so lines after the stopping point never run.

nodes.definition: Running a program under the debugger starts it paused just before its first line, so that the programmer decides how it goes on from there.

nodes.label: Program state
nodes.body: The state of a program is what the program holds at one moment: the values of its variables and the position of the line that is about to run. The chapter describes the debugger as a way to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). Each executed line can change the state, so a running program is a sequence of states, and the debugger lets the programmer stop the sequence and look at one of them.

paras.text: The state of a program is what the program holds at one moment: the values of its variables and the position of the line that is about to run. The chapter describes the debugger as a way to inspect the values in variables while the code runs and to track how the values change over the course of the program (Sweigart, 2025). Each executed line can change the state, so a running program is a sequence of states, and the debugger lets the programmer stop the sequence and look at one of them.

A bug is a state that is not the one the programmer expected, and a wrong state always comes from some line. The chapter contrasts seeing the actual values in a program while it runs with having to deduce what the values might be from the source code (Sweigart, 2025). Deduction can be wrong in exactly the places where the bug hides, whereas the state seen in the debugger is the real one. The skill of debugging is largely the skill of comparing the state that is shown with the state that was expected.

The chapter's coin program is a good example of state. After 500 of the 1,000 flips, the variable i holds 500 and the variable heads holds the number of heads so far, which the programmer wanted to read at the halfway point (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript, a breakpoint on the line print('Halfway done!') followed by the command c stops there, and p i prints 500. The state also includes which line comes next, which pdb shows with an arrow after each stop.

The state changes with every step. In the executed transcript of a two-line program that assigns x = 1 and then prints x, the command p x on line 1 prints *** NameError: name 'x' is not defined, because the line that creates x has not run yet; after the command n, p x prints 1. In a loop the state changes on every pass: with a breakpoint on the if line of the coin program, the first c stops with i equal to 1 and the second with i equal to 2.

The state is only what is true now. A pause shows the value that a variable has at that moment and not the values it had before, so a wrong value found at a pause may have been created many steps earlier. The programmer then has to run again with an earlier breakpoint, or step through the earlier lines while watching the value. A state that looks right also proves little, since the bug may show itself only with other values.

nodes.example: heads is 500 at the halfway point
nodes.definition: The state of a program at a moment is the values of its variables together with the line that is about to run; the debugger shows both.

nodes.label: Debug Inspector pane
nodes.body: The Debug Inspector pane is the part of the Mu window that lists the current value of each variable of the program. It opens at the right side of the window when the program is run under the debugger (Sweigart, 2025). Each row names a variable and shows the value that it has at this moment. When the program is paused, the pane is a snapshot of the variables, and it changes whenever the program moves on.

paras.text: The Debug Inspector pane is the part of the Mu window that lists the current value of each variable of the program. It opens at the right side of the window when the program is run under the debugger (Sweigart, 2025). Each row names a variable and shows the value that it has at this moment. When the program is paused, the pane is a snapshot of the variables, and it changes whenever the program moves on.

The pane is where the debugger answers the question that logging and assertions can only answer in advance: what is in the variables now. In the chapter's adding program, the pane shows that the variables first, second and third hold the string values '5', '3' and '42' instead of the integer values 5, 3 and 42, and that is the whole bug (Sweigart, 2025). The quote marks around the values are the evidence. Without them the pane would show 5, 3 and 42 and the problem would stay hidden.

In Mu the pane is shown beside the file editor throughout a debugging session, as in Figure 5-3 of the chapter. In pdb the same information is requested on demand with the command p followed by an expression, which prints the value of the expression in the current context (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript of a program that assigns first = '5', second = '3' and third = '42', the command p first prints '5' with its quote marks, and p first + second + third prints '5342'.

The pane lets the programmer test a theory before changing anything. In the adding program the theory is that adding the three variables joins their text, and the evidence is the quote marks. The cure follows from it: int() turns each string into a number, and in the executed transcript p int(first) + int(second) + int(third) prints 50. In pdb the command p can take any expression, so the same session can answer many questions about the state of the program without editing the file.
