The pane shows values, but a value alone can mislead. The text '5' and the number 5 look alike unless the display shows the quote marks,. Also, the pane shows the program as it is when paused and says nothing about how it got there, so the programmer should step through the preceding lines while watching the value change. In pdb, asking for a variable that has not been assigned yet prints an error line that says the name is not defined.

nodes.example: first, second and third shown as strings
nodes.definition: The pane at the right of the Mu window that lists the current value of each variable of the paused program.

nodes.label: Stop button
nodes.body: The Stop button ends a debugging session immediately. The chapter says that to stop debugging entirely, without bothering to execute the rest of the program, one clicks the Stop button, and that it immediately terminates the program (Sweigart, 2025). It is the usual Stop button of the editor, which is also available during debugging, next to the buttons that Debugging mode adds (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the equivalent is the quit command, which the documentation says aborts the program being executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The Stop button ends a debugging session immediately. The chapter says that to stop debugging entirely, without bothering to execute the rest of the program, one clicks the Stop button, and that it immediately terminates the program (Sweigart, 2025). It is the usual Stop button of the editor, which is also available during debugging, next to the buttons that Debugging mode adds (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the equivalent is the quit command, which the documentation says aborts the program being executed (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A debugging session can end before the program does, at the moment the answer is found. A student who has seen in the pane that a variable holds a string has no need to run the remaining lines, and may not want them to run at all if they would write a file or wait for further input. Stop is the control that says the session is over and the program should not go on, whereas Continue says the program should go on without the debugger's pauses.

In Mu the button is on the top row of the editor. In pdb the command is q or quit, and an end-of-file on the input has the same effect (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript of a program that prints a line called end after its last statement, giving the command q at the first stop prints nothing of the program at all, because it never reached the print, and the output ends with the (Pdb) prompt. In 3.14 the documentation adds that a confirmation prompt is shown if the debugger was invoked in inline mode, which is the mode that breakpoint() uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The two ways of leaving a session differ in what happens to the rest of the program. Continue runs the rest of the program at full speed, stopping only at breakpoints (Sweigart, 2025). Stop terminates it. With pdb there is a third case, in which the program reaches its end by itself: pdb then reports that the program finished and will be restarted and returns to the first line, ready for another run (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Stopping is not the same as finishing. A program stopped in the middle may have printed only part of its output, written only part of a file, or changed things that the rest of the program would have changed back. And stopping the debugger does not remove the bug: the programmer still has to edit the program and run it again.

nodes.definition: The Stop button ends the debugging session at once and terminates the program without running its remaining lines.

nodes.label: Controls
nodes.body: The controls are the means by which the programmer moves a paused program forward, or tells it where to pause. The chapter lists the buttons that Debugging mode adds to the editor: Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out (Sweigart, 2025). The fifth control is the breakpoint, a mark on a line that makes the program pause whenever it gets there. Every control answers the question of how far the program should run before it stops again.

paras.text: The controls are the means by which the programmer moves a paused program forward, or tells it where to pause. The chapter lists the buttons that Debugging mode adds to the editor: Continue, Step Over, Step In and Step Out (Sweigart, 2025). The fifth control is the breakpoint, a mark on a line that makes the program pause whenever it gets there. Every control answers the question of how far the program should run before it stops again.

A debugger is only as useful as the control the programmer has over it. Stepping through a long program one line at a time takes too long, and running it at full speed lets the interesting moment go by. The chapter shows how the controls divide the work: breakpoints and Continue skip the part of the program that is not of interest, and the steps examine the part that is. The chapter notes, for instance, that stepping through the 1,000 flips of its coin program would take thousands of clicks (Sweigart, 2025).

The controls are the buttons at the top of the Mu window, the entries of IDLE's debugger window, and the commands of pdb. The documentation of pdb names them step, next, return, continue and break, each also available in the short form s, n, r, c and b (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's questions at the end ask for exactly these differences between the three step buttons and for the moment at which Continue stops.

The concepts come in this order: the breakpoint, which places a pause in the program, Continue, which runs to the next pause, and the three steps, which move by a line, over a call, or out of a function. For each control the text gives the button of Mu, the command of pdb, and an executed transcript on a small program in which a function named double is defined on line 1 and called on line 5.

nodes.label: Breakpoint
nodes.body: A breakpoint is a mark on a line of code that makes the debugger pause whenever the program reaches that line. The chapter says that setting a breakpoint on a specific line forces the debugger to pause whenever the program execution reaches that line (Sweigart, 2025). In Mu the breakpoint is set by clicking the line number in the file editor, which makes a red dot appear next to the number, and it is removed by clicking the line number again (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A breakpoint is a mark on a line of code that makes the debugger pause whenever the program reaches that line. The chapter says that setting a breakpoint on a specific line forces the debugger to pause whenever the program execution reaches that line (Sweigart, 2025). In Mu the breakpoint is set by clicking the line number in the file editor, which makes a red dot appear next to the number, and it is removed by clicking the line number again (Sweigart, 2025).

Breakpoints solve the problem of speed. Stepping through the program with the debugger is helpful but can also be slow (Sweigart, 2025), and often the interesting moment is far from the start. The chapter's coin program flips a coin 1,000 times, and the question of interest is the value of heads at the halfway point, when 500 flips are done. With a breakpoint the program runs at full speed to that moment and stops there, where the clicking of Step Over thousands of times would otherwise be needed.

In the chapter the breakpoint is placed on the line print('Halfway done!'), inside the if statement that checks whether i is 500. In the executed transcript of that program, the pdb command b 7 sets a breakpoint on line 7 and prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:7; the command c then runs the loop and stops at line 7, and the command p i prints 500 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation describes break as setting a break at a given line number in the current file. IDLE has the same facility through a context menu and, as its documentation says, saves the breakpoints of a file in the user's .idlerc directory (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The line matters. The chapter points out that a breakpoint on the if statement itself would stop at every pass through the loop, because that line runs on every iteration, whereas a breakpoint on the line inside the if stops only when the execution enters the if clause (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript a breakpoint on line 4, the if line, followed by two c commands, stops with i equal to 2, so each pass stopped once. After a stop the programmer can use Continue, Step Over, Step In or Step Out as normal (Sweigart, 2025).

A breakpoint on a line that never runs never stops the program, and a breakpoint on a line that runs very often stops very often. In IDLE, the documentation says that breakpoints only have an effect when running under the debugger (Python Software Foundation, 2026), so a program started with the plain Run command ignores them. In IDLE the breakpoints of a file are kept in the .idlerc directory and not in the program file, so the saved program is unchanged. A line that holds no instruction cannot carry a breakpoint: in the executed transcript, b 5 on a blank line prints *** Blank or comment and sets nothing, while b 4 on the line before it prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:4.

nodes.example: a red dot at a line number
nodes.definition: A breakpoint marks a line at which the debugger pauses the running program so its variables can be read.

nodes.label: Continue control
nodes.body: Continue is the control that lets a paused program run at normal speed again. The chapter says that clicking Continue causes the program to execute normally until it terminates or reaches a breakpoint, and that someone who is done debugging and wants the program to go on normally should click it (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is continue, or c, and the documentation says it continues execution and stops only when a breakpoint is encountered (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Continue is the control that lets a paused program run at normal speed again. The chapter says that clicking Continue causes the program to execute normally until it terminates or reaches a breakpoint, and that someone who is done debugging and wants the program to go on normally should click it (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is continue, or c, and the documentation says it continues execution and stops only when a breakpoint is encountered (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Continue is the control that joins the two modes of work. Between breakpoints the programmer wants the program at full speed, and at a breakpoint the programmer wants it slowly. Without Continue, a debugging session would have to choose one or the other. With it, a session reads like a story: the program starts paused, Continue runs it up to the breakpoint, the programmer looks and steps, and Continue runs it up to the next one.

In the chapter's coin program the program starts in a paused state at the first line, as usual, and clicking Continue makes it run at full speed until it reaches the line with the breakpoint (Sweigart, 2025). The executed transcript shows the same: after b 7 the command c ends with the stop at line 7, with the 500 flips behind it. If a second c is given, there is no further breakpoint, so the program runs on, prints its last lines, and pdb reports that the program finished and will be restarted.

Continue stops for one of two reasons only: a breakpoint or the end of the program. If the same breakpoint is inside a loop, Continue stops again on every pass, and in the executed transcript of the breakpoint on the if line, the first c stopped at the first pass and the second c at the second. The chapter's last review question asks when the debugger stops after Continue, and the answer is just these two cases (Sweigart, 2025).

Continue is not Stop. It leaves the debugger attached, and a breakpoint that is later reached pauses the program again, while Stop ends the session. And Continue offers no protection against a program that never ends: a loop that never finishes runs forever under Continue if no breakpoint is hit. In that case the programmer must interrupt the program or use the Stop button.

nodes.definition: Continue runs the program until the next breakpoint or the end.

nodes.label: Step in
nodes.body: Step In is the control that executes the next line and then pauses again. The chapter adds that if the next line is a function call, the debugger steps into that function, jumping to the function's first line of code (Sweigart, 2025). The pdb command for the same control is step, or s, and the documentation says it executes the current line and stops at the first possible occasion, either in a function that is called or on the next line in the current function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Step In is the control that executes the next line and then pauses again. The chapter adds that if the next line is a function call, the debugger steps into that function, jumping to the function's first line of code (Sweigart, 2025). The pdb command for the same control is step, or s, and the documentation says it executes the current line and stops at the first possible occasion, either in a function that is called or on the next line in the current function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The control is for looking inside. When the value that arrives from a function call is wrong, the cause is either the arguments or the function, and Step In is how the programmer enters the function to find out which. It gives the finest view of a program, one line at a time through every call. The finest view is also the slowest, and the chapter therefore says that Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025).

In the executed transcript of the program that defines double on line 1 and calls it on line 5, the stops are line 1, line 4 and line 5. At line 5 the command s prints --Call-- and then > main.py(1)double() with -> def double(x):, so the debugger has entered the function and shows the name of the function in the place where <module> stood before. The word Call is how pdb marks a stop caused by entering a function.

Step In behaves differently depending on the line. On a line that is not a call, it does the same as Step Over: it executes the line and pauses at the next. On a line that calls a function written in the program, it enters. The chapter notes that Mu should prevent the debugger from entering Python's built-in functions (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of pdb on a program whose lines 1 and 2 call print(), the command s on line 1 prints a and stops on line 2, so it did not enter print().

Step In on the wrong line leads into code that does not matter. The chapter warns about this with its adding program: the reader should use Step Over instead of Step In on the line that calls print(), because there is no interest in the code of print() (Sweigart, 2025). And once inside a function, the programmer must remember to get out again, with Step Out, or continue stepping through the lines of the function until it returns.

nodes.definition: Step In executes the next line and, if that line is a call, pauses on the first line of the called function.

nodes.label: Step over
nodes.body: Step Over is the control that executes the next line of code like Step In does, but treats a function call as a single step. The chapter says that, if the next line calls a function, Step Over steps over, or rushes through, the code in the function: its code runs at full speed and the debugger pauses as soon as the call returns (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is next, or n, and the documentation says that the difference between next and step is that step stops inside a called function, while next executes called functions at nearly full speed, stopping only at the next line in the current function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Step Over is the control that executes the next line of code like Step In does, but treats a function call as a single step. The chapter says that, if the next line calls a function, Step Over steps over, or rushes through, the code in the function: its code runs at full speed and the debugger pauses as soon as the call returns (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is next, or n, and the documentation says that the difference between next and step is that step stops inside a called function, while next executes called functions at nearly full speed, stopping only at the next line in the current function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Most of the time the programmer knows which functions work and wants to follow the main line of the program. The chapter's example is a call of a function named spam() whose inside does not matter: Step Over runs it and pauses when it returns, and the chapter concludes that for this reason Step Over is more common than Step In (Sweigart, 2025). The control keeps the session short and the attention on the code under suspicion.

In the adding program, the chapter uses Step Over for each of the print() and input() calls, from line 1 to the final print() on line 7, since stepping into the built-in functions would be pointless (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed transcript of the program with the function double, three n commands go from line 1 to line 4, to line 5 and to line 6, and after that the command p result prints 6. The call on line 5 ran completely in the third step, and the debugger never showed a stop inside the function.

The control is a decision about detail. By choosing Step Over on a line, the programmer says that the result of the line matters but how it was computed does not. If the result later turns out to be wrong, the programmer can start again, or use the breakpoint, and choose Step In on that line. The stops of the debugger stay in the same function, the one that is being examined, and each stop is the next line of that function.

Step Over hides what happens inside the call, including a bug. A function that has a mistake can return a wrong value, and Step Over will report only that the line finished. If an exception is raised inside the call, it is still raised: in the executed transcript, the command n on a line that calls a function whose body divides by zero prints ZeroDivisionError: division by zero and stays on the calling line. And when a line waits for typed input, the chapter notes that the highlighting goes away while Mu waits for the text (Sweigart, 2025).

nodes.definition: Step Over executes the next line as a whole, running a called function without pausing inside it.

nodes.label: Step out
nodes.body: Step Out is the control that runs the rest of the current function at full speed. The chapter says that it causes the debugger to execute lines of code at full speed until it returns from the current function, and that it is meant for the reader who has stepped into a function call with Step In and now simply wants to keep executing instructions until leaving it (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is return, or r, and the documentation says it continues execution until the current function returns (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: Step Out is the control that runs the rest of the current function at full speed. The chapter says that it causes the debugger to execute lines of code at full speed until it returns from the current function, and that it is meant for the reader who has stepped into a function call with Step In and now simply wants to keep executing instructions until leaving it (Sweigart, 2025). In pdb the command is return, or r, and the documentation says it continues execution until the current function returns (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The control repairs a step that went too deep. After Step In the programmer is on the first line of a function. If it turns out that the function is not under suspicion, walking through every one of its lines is a waste, and Step Out spends them at full speed. It is the counterpart of Step In in the way that going back is the counterpart of going forward, and it is used less than Step Over because a careful programmer steps in only where it is wanted.

In the executed transcript, the command s at line 5 enters the function double and stops on its first line, and the command r then prints --Return-- followed by > main.py(3)double()->6 and -> return y. The arrow and the number after it show that the function is about to return the value 6. The debugger has stopped on the return line, one step before control passes back to the caller, and one more step with n would continue in the calling code.

Step Out is therefore a way of saying finish this function. It does not skip the lines that follow in the caller. A breakpoint on a line of the function that has not yet run still stops the program first: in the executed transcript a breakpoint is set on line 2 of double after stepping into it, and the command r then stops on line 2 and not at the return. After the stop at the return, pdb shows the value that the function returns after the arrow, so the programmer can see the result before it is used.

Step Out from the top level, outside any function, has no function to leave. In the executed transcript the command r on line 1 of the program runs everything, so 6 and end are printed, and the stop is on the last line, where pdb prints --Return-- with ->None. The tools also differ in where they pause: the chapter speaks of executing at full speed until the function is left, and pdb pauses on the return line itself. The reader who needs the stop to be in the caller should take one more step.

nodes.definition: Step Out runs the rest of the current function at full speed until it returns.

nodes.label: Python debugger
nodes.body: The Python debugger is the debugger that comes with Python itself, the module pdb. The documentation says that pdb defines an interactive source code debugger for Python programs, with breakpoints, single stepping at the level of source lines, source code listing, and evaluation of Python code in the context of the paused program; it also supports post-mortem debugging, which means examining a program after it has crashed, and can be called under program control (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's controls all exist in it as commands.

paras.text: The Python debugger is the debugger that comes with Python itself, the module pdb. The documentation says that pdb defines an interactive source code debugger for Python programs, with breakpoints, single stepping at the level of source lines, source code listing, and evaluation of Python code in the context of the paused program; it also supports post-mortem debugging, which means examining a program after it has crashed, and can be called under program control (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's controls all exist in it as commands.

Unlike the buttons of an editor, pdb belongs to the standard library, so it comes with Python. It needs no window: the executed transcripts of this chapter were produced by starting it as a separate program and typing its commands as lines of input. It can be started in three ways: from the command line with python -m pdb followed by the file name, from inside the program by the function breakpoint(), and, since Python 3.14, by attaching to a process that is already running. The concepts below take the ways in turn.

The module is met whenever a Python program is run with python -m pdb, and whenever breakpoint() is reached. Its prompt is (Pdb). The documentation also shows the case of a program that has crashed: pdb.pm() can be called afterwards to enter the debugger at the place where the exception occurred and to print the value of a variable there (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Started as a module, pdb enters this post-mortem mode automatically if the program exits abnormally; in the executed transcript of a program that divides by zero on its second line, pdb prints Uncaught exception. Entering post mortem debugging and stops on that line.

The concepts of this group begin with the two ideas that the later ones depend on: the process, which is a running program, and the environment variable, a named setting handed to a program when it starts. They continue with the function breakpoint() and the hook that it calls, with the commands of pdb that correspond to the buttons of the chapter, and with attaching to a running process, which is new in Python 3.14.

nodes.label: Process
nodes.body: A process is a program that is running. PEP 768 speaks of running Python processes and of attaching to a live process by process ID (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024). The number that identifies a process is its process identifier, abbreviated PID, and the function os.getpid() returns the current process id (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The abbreviation appears in the options of pdb, where the documentation speaks of attaching to the process with the specified PID.

paras.text: A process is a program that is running. PEP 768 speaks of running Python processes and of attaching to a live process by process ID (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024). The number that identifies a process is its process identifier, abbreviated PID, and the function os.getpid() returns the current process id (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The abbreviation appears in the options of pdb, where the documentation speaks of attaching to the process with the specified PID.

The idea matters for debugging because running programs can be pointed at by number. A debugger that is started together with a program controls that one program. A debugger that attaches to a program that is already running needs to know which one, and the process identifier is the answer.

The process identifier is met in the command python -m pdb -p 1234 and in the call sys.remote_exec(1234, script) of Python 3.14 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed expression isinstance(os.getpid(), int) evaluates to True, and os.getpid() > 0 does too.

Two runs of Python are two processes even if they run the same file. The documentation of the subprocess module says that it allows a program to spawn new processes (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and a process spawned in this way has an identifier of its own: in the executed check, the number printed by the child differs from the number of the parent. A process also has an environment, which is the subject of the next concept.

The identifier belongs to one run only, since two runs are two processes. A tool that is pointed at a wrong number would examine another program, so the number should be read from the program itself, for example by printing os.getpid(), at the time it is needed.

nodes.definition: A process is a running program as the operating system sees it; each process has its own identifier, which os.getpid() returns.

nodes.label: Environment variable
nodes.body: An environment variable is a named piece of text that belongs to the environment in which a process runs. It belongs to the process environment, which the program can read. The documentation of the os module describes os.environ as a mapping object whose keys and values are strings that represent the process environment, with the example that environ['HOME'] is the path of the home directory on some platforms (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The glossary defines a mapping as a container object that supports arbitrary key lookups, and a dictionary is one (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: An environment variable is a named piece of text that belongs to the environment in which a process runs. It belongs to the process environment, which the program can read. The documentation of the os module describes os.environ as a mapping object whose keys and values are strings that represent the process environment, with the example that environ['HOME'] is the path of the home directory on some platforms (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The glossary defines a mapping as a container object that supports arbitrary key lookups, and a dictionary is one (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

Environment variables let a user change how a program behaves without editing it. For debugging this is valuable: the same program file can be run with its breakpoints active on one day and switched off on the next, and the file does not change. Python's own settings use the same means. The variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT, which is the subject of the following concepts, decides what the function breakpoint() does.

In os.environ, the executed expression type(os.environ).__name__ evaluates to '_Environ', the class that holds the environment. A program reads a variable with os.environ.get('NAME'), which gives None when the variable is not set; the executed check prints None for a name that is not set. The documentation also says that the mapping may be used to modify the environment, and the executed check shows that a variable assigned in os.environ is visible to a child process that is started afterwards (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The documentation says that the mapping is captured the first time the os module is imported, typically during Python startup, and that changes made to the environment after this time are not reflected in os.environ, except for changes made by modifying os.environ directly (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that changes os.environ changes the environment that it passes on: in the executed check the parent sets GREETING to hi and the child that is started next prints hi, while 'GREETING' in os.environ is True in the parent.

Values are text. The documentation says that keys and values are strings, so a setting such as 0 is the string '0', not the number zero (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It adds that on Windows the keys are converted to upper case, so a name written in lower case is stored in upper case there (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And a program that wants a value must handle its absence: os.environ.get('NAME') returns None when the variable is not set, but os.environ['NAME'] has no such default.

nodes.definition: A named text setting that the operating system hands to a process when it starts; Python reads it through os.environ.

nodes.label: Breakpoint function
nodes.body: The built-in function breakpoint() puts a breakpoint into the program itself. Writing breakpoint() on a line makes the program stop in the debugger when it reaches that line. The documentation of pdb says that, called with defaults, it can be used instead of import pdb; pdb.set_trace() (Python Software Foundation, 2026). PEP 553, which proposed the function, describes it as a new built-in that enters a Python debugger at the call site (Warsaw, 2017).

paras.text: The built-in function breakpoint() puts a breakpoint into the program itself. Writing breakpoint() on a line makes the program stop in the debugger when it reaches that line. The documentation of pdb says that, called with defaults, it can be used instead of import pdb; pdb.set_trace() (Python Software Foundation, 2026). PEP 553, which proposed the function, describes it as a new built-in that enters a Python debugger at the call site (Warsaw, 2017).

PEP 553 lists the disadvantages of the older idiom: it is a lot to type (27 characters), it is easy to mistype, and it ties debugging directly to the choice of pdb (Warsaw, 2017). The new function is short, and because it does not name pdb, the debugger that it starts can be chosen without changing the program. The PEP adds that even where an editor has a user interface for setting breakpoints, it may still be more convenient to just edit the code (Warsaw, 2017).

The function is used in scripts, and the pdb page of the documentation shows an example in which breakpoint() is the first line of a function double, followed by a session in which p x prints 3 and continue lets the program finish (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed run of a small program that prints before, calls breakpoint() and then prints after, the output contains before, then a (Pdb) prompt, and, after the command c, the word after.

The function does little itself. It calls sys.breakpointhook(), passing on whatever arguments it received, and returns what the hook returns (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The default hook starts pdb at the line after the call. The function therefore behaves as the hook decides, which the next concept explains. The executed expression sys.breakpointhook.__name__ evaluates to 'breakpointhook', the default hook that breakpoint() calls.

A breakpoint() that is left in the program will stop it for whoever runs it, including users who have no one to type commands. It should be removed before the program is shared, or switched off with the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, for which the executed run prints before and then the program went on without any pause. The documentation also says that if sys.breakpointhook cannot be reached, breakpoint() raises RuntimeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And since the default hook starts pdb.set_trace(), which expects no arguments, calling breakpoint(1) raises a TypeError, as the executed check shows.

nodes.definition: The built-in breakpoint() pauses the program in the debugger at that line; it calls sys.breakpointhook, and PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 makes it do nothing.

nodes.label: Breakpoint hook
nodes.body: The breakpoint hook is the function that breakpoint() calls: sys.breakpointhook. A hook is a name that holds a function which other code calls, so replacing the function changes what happens. The documentation says that by default the hook drops the programmer into the pdb debugger, but it can be set to any other function so that a different debugger is used (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This is the design of PEP 553, which proposed the hook and the environment variable together (Warsaw, 2017).

paras.text: The breakpoint hook is the function that breakpoint() calls: sys.breakpointhook. A hook is a name that holds a function which other code calls, so replacing the function changes what happens. The documentation says that by default the hook drops the programmer into the pdb debugger, but it can be set to any other function so that a different debugger is used (Python Software Foundation, 2026). This is the design of PEP 553, which proposed the hook and the environment variable together (Warsaw, 2017).

A hook lets one line of code, breakpoint(), serve many debuggers. A programmer who prefers another debugger can set the hook once, and the programs need not change. The environment variable also lets the person who runs the program turn the call off. The default hook consults PYTHONBREAKPOINT: if it is set to 0, the hook returns at once and does nothing; if it is not set or is empty, pdb.set_trace() is called; otherwise the variable names a function to call, in the dotted form package.module.function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The executed runs show each case. With PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, a program that prints before, calls breakpoint() and prints the program went on shows no pause. With PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to builtins.print, breakpoint('hello', 'hook') prints hello hook, because the named function receives the arguments that were passed. And a program that assigns its own function to sys.breakpointhook has that function called, with its arguments, and breakpoint() returns what the function returns.

The environment variable is read each time the default hook is called. If it names something that cannot be imported, the documentation says a RuntimeWarning is reported and the breakpoint is ignored (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed run, with PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to no.such.module.func, the error output ends with RuntimeWarning: Ignoring unimportable $PYTHONBREAKPOINT: 'no.such.module.func', and the program carries on, printing went on.

A program that replaces sys.breakpointhook by its own function no longer consults PYTHONBREAKPOINT, as the documentation says; in the executed run the replaced hook still ran with the variable set to 0 (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And the setting 0 silences only breakpoint(): in the executed transcript, with PYTHONBREAKPOINT set to 0, the command b 2 inside pdb still stops the program on line 2.

nodes.definition: The function sys.breakpointhook is what breakpoint() calls; by default it starts pdb, but the environment variable PYTHONBREAKPOINT or a replacement function can change it.

nodes.label: Pdb commands
nodes.body: The commands of pdb are the text form of the controls of the chapter. At the prompt (Pdb) the programmer types a command and presses Enter. The commands that correspond to the buttons are step (Step In), next (Step Over), return (Step Out), continue (Continue) and break (Breakpoint), and the command quit corresponds to the Stop button (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Each also has a short form, s, n, r, c, b and q.

paras.text: The commands of pdb are the text form of the controls of the chapter. At the prompt (Pdb) the programmer types a command and presses Enter. The commands that correspond to the buttons are step (Step In), next (Step Over), return (Step Out), continue (Continue) and break (Breakpoint), and the command quit corresponds to the Stop button (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Each also has a short form, s, n, r, c, b and q.

The commands make the controls of the chapter available in a terminal and in scripts, and they add to them. The command p expression evaluates an expression in the current context and prints its value, so it does the work of the Debug Inspector pane. The command where prints a stack trace with the most recent frame at the bottom and an arrow marking the current frame, which is the call stack of Chapter 4 viewed from the debugger (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The command list shows 11 lines of source code around the current line, with -> marking the current line (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

In the executed transcripts every control of the chapter appears as a command: n and s give the stops on lines 4 and 5 and then --Call-- at the start of double; r gives --Return-- and the value 6; b 6 prints Breakpoint 1 at main.py:6, and c stops there, where p result prints 6. The check on the class Pdb confirms that the six methods do_step, do_next, do_return, do_continue, do_break and do_where exist, which is the evaluated io example of this concept.

The commands steer the paused program, and a statement written after an exclamation point is executed in its context; the point can be omitted unless the first word of the statement resembles a debugger command (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation says that print() can also be used, but it is not a debugger command and executes the Python print() function (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The command-line form python -m pdb [-c command] file starts the program paused at the first line, and -c runs commands as if they were in a .pdbrc file (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

A name that matches a command is read as the command: the documentation says the exclamation point can be omitted only unless the first word resembles a debugger command (Python Software Foundation, 2026). In the executed transcript a variable called c holds 5, and p c prints 5, whereas typing c alone is the command continue and the program ran on to its end. Before a variable has been assigned, p prints an error line: p x on line 1 of a program that assigns x on that line prints *** NameError: name 'x' is not defined.

nodes.example: step, next, return, continue, break, where
nodes.definition: The standard debugger pdb offers the chapter's controls as commands: step, next, return, continue and break, and where lists the call stack.

nodes.label: Remote attach
nodes.body: Remote attach is the ability of the debugger to join a program that is already running. Since Python 3.14 the command python -m pdb -p 1234 attaches to the process with that PID (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It rests on the function sys.remote_exec(pid, script), which executes a file of Python code in the process with the given identifier (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and on PEP 768, which proposed a safe external debugger interface for CPython (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024).

paras.text: Remote attach is the ability of the debugger to join a program that is already running. Since Python 3.14 the command python -m pdb -p 1234 attaches to the process with that PID (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It rests on the function sys.remote_exec(pid, script), which executes a file of Python code in the process with the given identifier (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and on PEP 768, which proposed a safe external debugger interface for CPython (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024).

PEP 768 states the need: developers often need to analyze application behavior without stopping or restarting services, which is especially crucial for high-availability systems, and very few Python tools could attach to running processes (Galindo Salgado, Wozniski and Stojanovic, 2024). The What's New page for 3.14 calls the new interface a crucial capability for high-availability systems and production environments, since tools can inspect and interact with Python applications in real time (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The interface is used by debuggers and other tools, and the documented command is python -m pdb -p followed by the number of the process. The function sys.remote_exec is available on Unix and Windows (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The executed demonstration starts a child program that prints ready and then sleeps; the parent calls sys.remote_exec on its identifier with a script that prints injected, and the child's output then contains injected. On a Python older than 3.14 the function does not exist, so there is nothing to call.

The function returns at once, and the code is run by the main thread of the target process at the next available opportunity; there is no interface to learn when it ran, and the caller must keep the file in place until it has (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The target must run the same major and minor version of CPython as the caller (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The documentation of pdb adds that a process blocked in a system call or waiting for I/O attaches only once the next bytecode instruction is executed, and the glossary defines bytecode as the internal representation of a Python program in the CPython interpreter (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The same power is a risk, since a tool that can run code in another process could be misused, so the feature can be disabled: with the environment variable PYTHON_DISABLE_REMOTE_DEBUG, with the option -X disable-remote-debug, or at build time with --without-remote-debug (Python Software Foundation, 2026). It also needs the same version on both sides. The runnable example of this concept is deliberately small: it checks only that sys.breakpointhook is callable, because attaching needs a second running process of the same version and cannot be shown in one expression.

nodes.definition: Since Python 3.14 the debugger can attach to a running process by its identifier, using sys.remote_exec.

nodes.label: Modern practice
nodes.body: Modern practice is the part of the chapter in which the four instruments, exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger, are used together on programs that contain real mistakes. The chapter does this three times. It repairs a factorial function with the help of log messages, it finds why an adding program prints a wrong sum with the help of the debugger, and it ends with a practice program, a coin toss guessing game that the author says has multiple bugs in it, to be found by running the program a few times (Sweigart, 2025). The word modern points to the tools of current Python, which the other branches describe one by one.

paras.text: Modern practice is the part of the chapter in which the four instruments, exceptions, assertions, logging and the debugger, are used together on programs that contain real mistakes. The chapter does this three times. It repairs a factorial function with the help of log messages, it finds why an adding program prints a wrong sum with the help of the debugger, and it ends with a practice program, a coin toss guessing game that the author says has multiple bugs in it, to be found by running the program a few times (Sweigart, 2025). The word modern points to the tools of current Python, which the other branches describe one by one.

Knowing what an instrument does is not yet knowing when to use it. A learner who has read about the debugger still has to decide, faced with a program that prints the wrong number, whether to print values, to add a check or to step through the lines. The practice cases give that decision a concrete setting. The chapter's own advice is that, in general, the earlier you catch bugs, the easier they will be to fix (Sweigart, 2025), and a worked case shows what catching a bug early looks like in a real program.

The cases are met in the chapter's three programs and in the programs a learner writes afterwards. A loop that starts at the wrong number, a running total that begins with the wrong value, input that arrives as text instead of numbers, a random number that is compared with a word, and a test of membership applied to the wrong kind of value all appear in programs of a few lines. Each of these has a name in this branch and a short executed example.

The branch has one group, the worked cases. Each case names a kind of mistake, shows the symptom that it produces, shows the evidence that exposes it and states the repair. The first two cases, the off-by-one range and the starting value of an accumulator, belong to the factorial. The third, string concatenation, belongs to the adding program. The last three, the random integer, the membership test and the type mismatch comparison, belong to the coin toss game. The cases are exercises in reading evidence, and the evidence is always a value that is not the one expected.

A case is a pattern and not a recipe. The same symptom can have several causes: a total of zero can come from a loop that starts at zero, but also from a running total that was started at zero when a product was meant. The repair that fits one program may be wrong for the next one. The cases also do not replace testing; they train the eye for the evidence, and the evidence has to be produced by running the program.

nodes.label: Worked cases
nodes.body: The worked cases are six small mistakes, each taken from one of the programs of the chapter. A case consists of the faulty line, the symptom that the program shows, the instrument that exposes the cause, and the repair. Most of the cases produce no error message at all, which makes them logic errors; two of them, the ordering comparison and the membership test on a string, show an error message when the same mistake is pushed a little further.

paras.text: The worked cases are six small mistakes, each taken from one of the programs of the chapter. A case consists of the faulty line, the symptom that the program shows, the instrument that exposes the cause, and the repair. Most of the cases produce no error message at all, which makes them logic errors; two of them, the ordering comparison and the membership test on a string, show an error message when the same mistake is pushed a little further.

The cases are useful in three ways. They show how each instrument is used on a real program and not on an artificial one. They give the learner a stock of patterns to recognise, which shortens the search the next time. And they fix the vocabulary: to say that a bug is an off-by-one in a range, or a type mismatch in a comparison, is to say where to look. In the chapter the logging output pointed at the range, and the debugger pane at the strings.

The cases follow the order of the chapter's programs. The off-by-one range and the accumulator starting value explain the factorial that returns 0. String concatenation explains the adding program, whose pane shows '5', '3' and '42' as strings. The random integer, the membership test and the type mismatch comparison explain the lines of the coin toss game that decide whether the player's guess is accepted and whether it matches. For each case the executed examples show the value that exposes the mistake.

The six cases share one shape, and the numbers make that shape concrete. A factorial whose accumulator starts at 0 prints 0 for every input, while one whose loop runs over range(1, n) instead of range(1, n + 1) prints 24 where 120 was wanted for an input of 5. The adding program prints 5342 because '5', '3' and '42' are strings and the plus sign joins them, whereas converting each with int before the addition prints 50 (Sweigart, 2025). Every case is therefore a wrong number rather than a message, which is why the instrument that exposes it has to be chosen deliberately instead of waited for.

nodes.label: Off-by-one range
nodes.body: An off-by-one error is a loop that runs one step too many, one too few, or from the wrong first number. The chapter's example is the factorial function, which contains the line for i in range(n + 1). The built-in type range is documented with the form range(start, stop), and the documentation says that if the start argument is omitted, it defaults to 0, and that the contents are the numbers from start up to but not including stop (Python Software Foundation, 2026). So range(n + 1) gives the numbers from 0 to n, and the factorial needs the numbers from 1 to n.

paras.text: An off-by-one error is a loop that runs one step too many, one too few, or from the wrong first number. The chapter's example is the factorial function, which contains the line for i in range(n + 1). The built-in type range is documented with the form range(start, stop), and the documentation says that if the start argument is omitted, it defaults to 0, and that the contents are the numbers from start up to but not including stop (Python Software Foundation, 2026). So range(n + 1) gives the numbers from 0 to n, and the factorial needs the numbers from 1 to n.

The error is easy to make because the counting rules of ranges are not the counting rules of everyday speech. People count from 1 and include the last number, and range counts from 0 by default and leaves the last number out. A programmer who writes range(n + 1) has remembered that the last number is left out and added 1 to make up for it, but forgot that the first number is 0. The mistake produces no error message: the program runs and prints 0, which the chapter calls a result that isn't right (Sweigart, 2025).

The log in the chapter shows the evidence. The debug messages say i is 0, total is 0 on the first pass, and then total stays 0 on every pass because zero times anything is zero (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed program, factorial(5) with range(n + 1) prints 0, and with range(1, n + 1) it prints 120. The two ranges are visible directly: list(range(5 + 1)) is [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], list(range(1, 5 + 1)) is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], and range(0) is empty.

The repair changes the first number of the range. With range(1, n + 1) the loop variable i takes the values 1 to n, and the log of the chapter then shows i and total as 1 and 1, 2 and 2, 3 and 6, 4 and 24, and 5 and 120 (Sweigart, 2025). The number of passes matters as much as their values: len(range(5 + 1)) is 6, one more than the 5 that len(range(1, 5 + 1)) gives, and the first pass was the harmful one. In the executed check factorial(0) and factorial(1) both give 1 after the repair, as the mathematical definition requires.

Counting errors hide in the edges. An off-by-one error can show itself only for the first or the last item, so tests should use the smallest case, the case with one item, and the case with none. A repair that adds or subtracts 1 until the output looks right is dangerous; the right question is which numbers the loop should visit, and the answer should be written down before the range. Watching the first and last pass in a log or in the debugger is the quickest check.

nodes.definition: The chapter's factorial multiplies by zero because its range starts at 0; the log shows i as 0 and total as 0 on the first pass, and range(1, n + 1) fixes it.

nodes.label: Accumulator starting value
nodes.body: The starting value of an accumulator is the value it holds before the loop begins. An accumulator, as Chapter 3 introduced it, is a variable that collects a result over the passes of a loop: it is given a starting value, and each pass updates it with the item of that pass. The chapter's factorial contains one: total = 1 before the loop and total *= i inside it (Sweigart, 2025). The line total *= i is an augmented assignment, which the language reference describes as evaluating the target and the expression, performing the operation on the two operands, and assigning the result to the original target (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: The starting value of an accumulator is the value it holds before the loop begins. An accumulator, as Chapter 3 introduced it, is a variable that collects a result over the passes of a loop: it is given a starting value, and each pass updates it with the item of that pass. The chapter's factorial contains one: total = 1 before the loop and total *= i inside it (Sweigart, 2025). The line total *= i is an augmented assignment, which the language reference describes as evaluating the target and the expression, performing the operation on the two operands, and assigning the result to the original target (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The starting value is part of the logic of the program, and a wrong one gives a wrong answer without any error. A product must start with 1, because multiplying by 1 changes nothing, and a sum must start with 0, because adding 0 changes nothing. A product that starts with 0 stays 0, and a sum that starts with 1 comes out one too large. The starting value is a place where a logic error can live, since the loop looks right and only the line before it is wrong.

Accumulators appear in nearly every program that totals, counts or builds a result. In the executed examples, a loop that adds the numbers 1 to 5 to a total that starts at 0 gives 15; the same loop with the total starting at 1 gives 16; and a loop that multiplies the numbers 1 to 5 into a total that starts at 0 gives 0, the same wrong answer as the chapter's factorial, though here the cause is the starting value and not the range. The built-in sum(range(1, 5 + 1)) evaluates to 15 and checks the first result.

The update line works in the same way on every pass: it takes the current value, combines it with the item, and stores the result back. The statement x += 1 can be rewritten as x = x + 1 to achieve a similar, but not exactly equal, effect, because the augmented form evaluates x only once (Python Software Foundation, 2026). After the loop the accumulator holds the result. To check one, the programmer can print it inside the loop, as the chapter does with its log messages, or can set a breakpoint on the update line and read the value on each pass.

When a total comes out wrong, there are two suspects, the loop and the starting value, and both must be checked before anything is changed. Another trap is to initialise the accumulator inside the loop, which resets it on every pass and leaves only the last item. And the type of the accumulator matters: the same update written with + on strings joins text, as in the next case, instead of adding numbers.

nodes.definition: The value that an accumulator holds before its loop must suit the operation: 1 for a product, 0 for a sum; a wrong start gives a wrong result without any error.

nodes.label: String concatenation
nodes.body: String concatenation is the joining of strings, written with the plus sign. The Python documentation lists the operation s + t as the concatenation of s and t (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When the operands are numbers the plus sign adds them, and when they are strings it joins them, so '5' + '3' is '53', and the result has no error and no warning. The chapter's adding program shows the consequence: it prints The sum is 5342 for the inputs 5, 3 and 42 (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: String concatenation is the joining of strings, written with the plus sign. The Python documentation lists the operation s + t as the concatenation of s and t (Python Software Foundation, 2026). When the operands are numbers the plus sign adds them, and when they are strings it joins them, so '5' + '3' is '53', and the result has no error and no warning. The chapter's adding program shows the consequence: it prints The sum is 5342 for the inputs 5, 3 and 42 (Sweigart, 2025).

The case matters because the data that input() returns is always text. The documentation of input() says that the function reads a line from input, converts it to a string, and returns that (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A program that asks a person for numbers therefore holds strings, and the programmer sees the digits and takes them for numbers. The chapter's Debug Inspector pane makes the difference visible: the variables first, second and third are set to '5', '3' and '42' instead of 5, 3 and 42, and when the last line is executed Python concatenates the strings instead of adding the numbers (Sweigart, 2025).

In the executed program the three answers are read with input(), and print('The sum is ' + first + second + third) prints The sum is 5342, while converting each answer with int() gives 50. The types can be read directly: type(input()).__name__ is 'str' even when the line typed was 7. The multiplication sign shows the same difference, since '5' * 3 is '555' and 5 * 3 is 15. And mixing the two kinds fails: adding a string and a number raises a TypeError, whose message for 'The sum is ' + 5 is can only concatenate str (not 'int') to str.

The cure is to convert before computing. The function int() turns a string of digits into an integer, so int(first) + int(second) + int(third) is the sum that was meant. The debugger shows the cure at work: in the pdb transcript of the adding program, p first + second + third prints '5342' and p int(first) + int(second) + int(third) prints 50. A conversion done right after the input call keeps the rest of the program working with numbers.

Conversion has its own failure: int() applied to a string that is not made of digits raises a ValueError, so a check on the input belongs near the input call. The quote marks in the display of a value are the most reliable sign that it is a string, and the debugger shows them where print() does not: print(first) shows 5, and the pane shows '5'.

nodes.definition: input and a list of typed answers give strings, and adding strings joins them, so the sum prints as 5342 until each answer is converted with int.

nodes.label: Random integer
nodes.body: A random integer is a whole number chosen by chance from a range. The function random.randint(a, b) returns a random integer N such that a <= N <= b, and the documentation adds that it is an alias, another name, for randrange(a, b+1) (Python Software Foundation, 2026), where randrange(start, stop) returns a randomly selected element from range(start, stop) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The two ends are both possible, which is different from range, whose last number is left out. In the chapter's programs randint(0, 1) simulates a coin flip, where the book says it returns 0 half of the time and 1 the other half (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: A random integer is a whole number chosen by chance from a range. The function random.randint(a, b) returns a random integer N such that a <= N <= b, and the documentation adds that it is an alias, another name, for randrange(a, b+1) (Python Software Foundation, 2026), where randrange(start, stop) returns a randomly selected element from range(start, stop) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The two ends are both possible, which is different from range, whose last number is left out. In the chapter's programs randint(0, 1) simulates a coin flip, where the book says it returns 0 half of the time and 1 the other half (Sweigart, 2025).

Chance is useful in programs that simulate, shuffle or play games, and it makes debugging harder, because a bug may show itself on one run and not on the next. The chapter's coin program therefore prints a different count each time: the book shows 490 heads in one run (Sweigart, 2025). A programmer who wants a repeatable run can call random.seed, which the documentation describes as initialising the random number generator (Python Software Foundation, 2026); in the executed check, two runs seeded with 1 give the same five numbers.

The coin flip in the chapter calls random.randint(0, 1) a thousand times and counts the ones as heads. The practice program calls it once, in toss = random.randint(0, 1), with the comment that 0 is tails and 1 is heads (Sweigart, 2025). In the executed checks, randint(5, 5) always returns 5, because the two ends are the same; randint(1, 3) over 500 calls produced exactly the numbers 1, 2 and 3; and the values are integers, so isinstance(random.randint(1, 6), int) is True and the type is int, not str.

The function needs the first number not to be larger than the second. In the executed check, random.randint(2, 1) raises a ValueError whose message begins empty range in. Under Python 3.14 the message ends with randint(2, 1), and under Python 3.12 it ends with randrange(2, 2), which shows the documented alias at work: randint(a, b) is randrange(a, b + 1) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A coin flip is a choice between two numbers, and the program must decide what each number means: here 0 stands for tails and 1 for heads, and nothing in the number itself says so.

The result is a number and not a word. A program that compares it with a string, as the practice program does, will never find them equal, which is the last of the worked cases. The random values are also not guaranteed to balance: the book's own run printed 490 heads in 1,000 flips, not 500 (Sweigart, 2025). And a breakpoint at the halfway point of such a program shows a different value of the counter on every run.

nodes.definition: random.randint(a, b) returns a random whole number N with a <= N <= b, both ends included.

nodes.label: Membership test
nodes.body: A membership test asks whether a value is among the members of a collection. The operators in and not in do it: the language reference says x in s evaluates to True if x is a member of s and False otherwise, and x not in s is the negation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's practice program uses the test to repeat a question until the answer is acceptable: while guess not in ('heads', 'tails'). The collection in the parentheses is a tuple, which the tutorial describes as a number of values separated by commas, and which is immutable, that is, cannot be changed once made (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: A membership test asks whether a value is among the members of a collection. The operators in and not in do it: the language reference says x in s evaluates to True if x is a member of s and False otherwise, and x not in s is the negation (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter's practice program uses the test to repeat a question until the answer is acceptable: while guess not in ('heads', 'tails'). The collection in the parentheses is a tuple, which the tutorial describes as a number of values separated by commas, and which is immutable, that is, cannot be changed once made (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The test replaces a chain of comparisons with one readable condition. Without it the loop would have to say guess != 'heads' and guess != 'tails', and a third answer would lengthen the line. For strings the operator means something else: the language reference says that for the string types x in y is True if and only if x is a substring of y (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Both meanings are useful, and mixing them up is the source of a typical mistake.

In the practice program the test works as intended. In the executed run with the inputs maybe, tails and tails, the question Guess the coin toss! Enter heads or tails: is printed twice, once for maybe, which is not a member of the tuple, and once for tails, which is. The difference between the two meanings is visible in the checks: 'ab' in 'abc' is True because it is a substring, 'head' in 'heads' is True, but 'head' in ('heads', 'tails') is False because 'head' is not a member of the tuple.

The two sides of the operator must fit. A string on the right accepts only strings on the left, and the check 1 in 'abc' raises a TypeError with the message 'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not int. A tuple on the right accepts any value, and the test uses equality, so 0 in (0, 1) is True and '0' in (0, 1) is False. A single value in parentheses is not a tuple: the check type(('heads')).__name__ gives 'str', and type(('heads',)).__name__ gives 'tuple', because the comma makes the tuple (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

One error to watch for is forgetting the comma. With guess in ('heads') the test asks whether guess is a substring of the word heads, so the answer 'he' is accepted. A second trap is to write the test as guess == 'heads' or 'tails', which is true for every guess, because a string that is not empty counts as true when it is used as a condition (Python Software Foundation, 2026); in the executed check the expression 'x' == 'heads' or 'tails' evaluates to 'tails', which is true. The membership operator avoids both.

nodes.definition: The in and not in operators test whether a value is a member of a collection; for a string they test whether one string is a substring of another.

error.out: TypeError: 'in <string>' requires string as left operand, not int

nodes.label: Type mismatch comparison
nodes.body: A type mismatch comparison compares two values of different kinds, such as a number and a string. The documentation of the built-in types says that unless stated otherwise, objects of different types never compare equal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). So 0 == 'heads' is False and 0 != 'heads' is True, without any error, however the values are chosen. This is the bug at the centre of the chapter's practice program: toss = random.randint(0, 1) is an integer and guess is a string, and the test if toss == guess can never be true.

paras.text: A type mismatch comparison compares two values of different kinds, such as a number and a string. The documentation of the built-in types says that unless stated otherwise, objects of different types never compare equal (Python Software Foundation, 2026). So 0 == 'heads' is False and 0 != 'heads' is True, without any error, however the values are chosen. This is the bug at the centre of the chapter's practice program: toss = random.randint(0, 1) is an integer and guess is a string, and the test if toss == guess can never be true.

The mistake is silent and total. The program runs, asks its questions, and answers Nope! to every guess, the correct one too. Nothing is raised and nothing is logged. The only evidence is the behaviour: the executed run with the inputs heads and heads prints Nope! Guess again! and then Nope. You are really bad at this game., and a player who guesses for ever is never right. The case shows why the chapter calls the program one with multiple bugs in it, to be found by running it a few times (Sweigart, 2025).

The comparison appears wherever data arrives in one form and is tested in another, as the number from randint and the word typed by the player do. The ordering operators are stricter than equality: the language reference says a default order comparison is not provided and an attempt raises TypeError (Python Software Foundation, 2026), and in the executed check 0 < 'heads' raises a TypeError with the message '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'str'. Equality asks only whether the values are the same and answers no, while ordering asks which is larger and cannot answer.

The repair is to compare like with like. Either the number is turned into the word, as in ['tails', 'heads'][toss], which gives 'heads' for 1 and 'tails' for 0, or the word is turned into the number. The program's own comment says that 0 is tails and 1 is heads, and the comment states exactly the mapping that the code has to carry out. The check can be made with p toss == guess in the debugger or with a temporary print of both values and their types.

A correct-looking condition is not evidence. A program that prints Nope for every input should lead the programmer to print the two operands and their types, not to read the condition again. The mismatch can also stand in a place where the comparison is spread over lines or functions, so that the two values never appear together. Also remember that numbers of different types do compare, since a comparison between numbers of different types behaves as though the exact values were compared (Python Software Foundation, 2026): 1 == 1.0 is True, so the rule concerns kinds that are unrelated, such as number and string.

nodes.definition: A number never equals a string, so comparing the integer from randint with 'heads' is always false and the game reports every guess as wrong.
